entries.2f9dfe204562af761a9146ef20ca959e1cf03322: <div sID="gen31301" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="1Cor.14" sID="1Cor.14"/> <div eID="gen31301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31302" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31303" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle directs them about the use of their spiritual gifts, preferring those that are best and fitted to do the greatest good. I. He begins with advising them of all spiritual gifts to prefer prophesying, and shows that this is much better than speaking with tongues, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1-1Cor.14.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. He goes on to show them how unprofitable the speaking of foreign languages is, and useless to the church; it is like piping in one tone, like sounding a trumpet without any certain note, like talking gibberish; whereas gifts should be used for the good of the church, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.6-1Cor.14.14">ver. 6-14</reference>. III. He advises that worship should be celebrated so that the most ignorant might understand, and join in prayer and praise, and presses the advice by his own example, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.15-1Cor.14.20">ver. 15-20</reference>. IV. He informs them that tongues were a sign for unbelievers rather than those that believe; and represents the advantage of prophecy above speaking with tongues, from the different suggestions they would give to the mind of an unbeliever coming into their assemblies, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.21-1Cor.14.25">ver. 21-25</reference>. V. He blames them for the disorder and confusion they had brought into the assembly, by their vanity and ostentation of their gifts; and directs them in using the gifts both of tongues and prophecy, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.26-1Cor.14.33">ver. 26-33</reference>. VI. He forbids women speaking in the church; and closes this subject by requiring them to perform every thing in the public worship with order and decency, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34-1Cor.14.40">ver. 34, to the end</reference>.
entries.eb1e472348dc64ad704bcd789bc54751f1feda93: <div eID="gen31303" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31302" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">On Spiritual Gifts. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31304" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Follow after charity, and desire spiritual <hi type="italic">gifts,</hi> but rather that ye may prophesy. <hi type="super">2</hi> For he that speaketh in an <hi type="italic">unknown</hi> tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth <hi type="italic">him;</hi> howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries. <hi type="super">3</hi> But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men <hi type="italic">to</hi> edification, and exhortation, and comfort. <hi type="super">4</hi> He that speaketh in an <hi type="italic">unknown</hi> tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church. 5 I would that ye all spake with tongues, but rather that ye prophesied: for greater <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that prophesieth than he that speaketh with tongues, except he interpret, that the church may receive edifying. <div eID="gen31304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31305" type="x-p"/> The apostle, in the foregoing chapter, had himself preferred, and advised the Corinthians to prefer, Christian charity to all spiritual gifts. Here he teaches them, among spiritual gifts, which they should prefer, and by what rules they should make comparison. He begins the chapter, <div eID="gen31305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31306" type="x-p"/> I. With an exhortation to charity (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Follow after charity,</hi> pursue it. The original, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">diokete,</hi></hi> when spoken of a thing, signifies a singular concern to obtain it; and is commonly taken in a good and laudable sense. It is an exhortation to obtain charity, to get this excellent disposition of mind upon any terms, whatever pains or prayers it may cost: as if he had said, "In whatever you fail, see you do not miss of this; the principal of all graces is worth your getting at any rate." <div eID="gen31306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31307" type="x-p"/> II. He directs them which spiritual gift to prefer, from a principle of charity: "<hi type="italic">Desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy,</hi> or chiefly that you may prophesy." While they were in close pursuit of charity, and made this Christian disposition their chief scope, they might be zealous of spiritual gifts, be ambitious of them in some measure, but especially of prophesying, that is, of interpreting scripture. This preference would most plainly discover that they were indeed upon such pursuit, that they had a due value for Christian charity, and were intent upon it. Note, Gifts are fit objects of our desire and pursuit, in subordination to grace and charity. That should be sought first and with the greatest earnestness which is most worth. <div eID="gen31307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31308" type="x-p"/> III. He assigns the reasons of this preference. And it is remarkable here that he only compares prophesying with speaking with tongues. It seems, this was the gift on which the Corinthians principally valued themselves. This was more ostentatious than the plain interpretation of scripture, more fit to gratify pride, but less fit to pursue the purposes of Christian charity; it would not equally edify nor do good to the souls of men. For, 1. He that spoke with tongues must wholly speak between God and himself; for, whatever mysteries might be communicated in his language, none of his own countrymen could understand them, because they did not understand the language, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, What cannot be understood can never edify. No advantage can be reaped from the most excellent discourses, if delivered in unintelligible language, such as the audience can neither speak nor understand: but he that prophesies speaks to the advantage of his hearers; they may profit by his gift. Interpretation of scripture will be for their edification; they may be exhorted and comforted by it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.3">v. 3</reference>. And indeed these two must go together. Duty is the proper way to comfort; and those that would be comforted must bear being exhorted. 2. He that speaks with tongues may edify himself, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.4">v. 4</reference>. He may understand and be affected with what he speaks; and so every minister should; and he that is most edified himself is in the disposition and fitness to do good to others by what he speaks; but he that speaks with tongues, or language unknown, can only edify himself; others can reap no benefit from his speech. Whereas the end of speaking in the church is to edify the church (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.4">v. 4</reference>), to which prophesying, or interpreting scripture by inspiration or otherwise, is immediately adapted. Note, That is the best and most eligible gift which best answers the purposes of charity and does most good; not that which can edify ourselves only, but that which will edify the church. Such is prophesying, or preaching, and interpreting scripture, compared with speaking in an unknown tongue. 3. Indeed, no gift is to be despised, but the best gifts are to be preferred. <hi type="italic">I could wish,</hi> says the apostle, <hi type="italic">that you all spoke with tongues, but rather that you prophesied,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.5">v. 5</reference>. Every gift of God is a favour from God, and may be improved for his glory, and as such is to be valued and thankfully received; but then those are to be most valued that are most useful. <hi type="italic">Greater is he that prophesieth than he that speaketh with tongues, unless he interpret, that the church may receive edifying,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.5">v. 5</reference>. Benevolence makes a man truly great. <hi type="italic">It is more blessed to give than to receive.</hi> And it is true magnanimity to study and seek to be useful to others, rather than to raise their admiration and draw their esteem. Such a man has a large soul, copious and diffused in proportion to his benevolence and bent of mind for public good. Greater is he who interprets scripture to edify the church than he who speaks tongues to recommend himself. And what other end he who spoke with tongues could have, unless he interpreted what he spoke, is not easy to say, Note, That makes most for the honour of a minister which is most for the church's edification, not that which shows his gifts to most advantage. He acts in a narrow sphere, while he aims at himself; but his spirit and character increase in proportion to his usefulness, I mean his own intention and endeavours to be useful.
entries.03b7eb0fa4198c19175e490ad7b32f9bfad13488: <div eID="gen31308" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">On Spiritual Gifts. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31309" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Now, brethren, if I come unto you speaking with tongues, what shall I profit you, except I shall speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophesying, or by doctrine? <hi type="super">7</hi> And even things without life giving sound, whether pipe or harp, except they give a distinction in the sounds, how shall it be known what is piped or harped? <hi type="super">8</hi> For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle? <hi type="super">9</hi> So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air. <hi type="super">10</hi> There are, it may be, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them <hi type="italic">is</hi> without signification. <hi type="super">11</hi> Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a barbarian unto me. <hi type="super">12</hi> Even so ye, forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual <hi type="italic">gifts,</hi> seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church. 13 Wherefore let him that speaketh in an <hi type="italic">unknown</hi> tongue pray that he may interpret. <hi type="super">14</hi> For if I pray in an <hi type="italic">unknown</hi> tongue, my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful. <div eID="gen31309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31310" type="x-p"/> In this paragraph he goes on to show how vain a thing the ostentation of speaking unknown and unintelligible language must be. It was altogether unedifying and unprofitable (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">If I come to you speaking with tongues, what will it profit you, unless I speak to you by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophesying, or by doctrine?</hi> It would signify nothing to utter any of these in an unknown tongue. An apostle, with all his furniture, could not edify, unless he spoke to the capacity of his hearers. New revelations, the most clear explications of old ones, the most instructive discourses in themselves, would be unprofitable in a language not understood. Nay, interpretations of scripture made in an unknown tongue would need to be interpreted over again, before they could be of any use. <div eID="gen31310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31311" type="x-p"/> I. He illustrates this by several allusions. 1. To a pipe and a harp playing always in one tone. Of what use can this be to those who are dancing? If there be no distinction of sounds, how should they order their steps or motions? Unintelligible language is like piping or harping without distinction of sounds: it gives no more direction how a man should order his conversation than a pipe with but one stop or a harp with but one string can direct a dancer how he should order his steps, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.7">v. 7</reference>. 2. To a trumpet giving an <hi type="italic">uncertain sound,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">adelon phonen,</hi></hi> a sound not manifest; either not the proper sound for the purpose, or not distinct enough to be discerned from every other sound. If, instead of sounding on onset, it sounded a retreat, or sounded one knew not what, who would prepare for the battle? To talk in an unknown language in a Christian assembly is altogether as vain and to no purpose as for a trumpet to give no certain sound in the field or day of battle. The army in one case, and the congregation in the other, must be all in suspense, and at a perfect nonplus. To speak words that have no significancy to those who hear them is to leave them ignorant of what is spoken; it is speaking to the air, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.9">v. 9</reference>. Words without a meaning can convey no notion nor instruction to the mind; and words not understood have no meaning with those who do not understand them: to talk to them in such language is to waste our breath. 3. He compares the speaking in an unknown tongue to the gibberish of barbarians. There are, as he says (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.10">v. 10</reference>), many kinds of voices in the world, none of which is without its proper signification. This is true of the several languages spoken by different nations. All of them have their proper signification. Without this they would be <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">phonai aphonoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a voice, and no voice.</hi> For that is no language, nor can it answer the end of speaking, which has no meaning. But whatever proper signification the words of any language may have in themselves, and to those who understand them, they are perfect gibberish to men of another language, who understand them not. In this case, speaker and hearers are barbarians to each other (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.11">v. 11</reference>), they talk and hear only sounds without sense; for this is to be a barbarian. For thus says the polite Ovid, when banished into Pontus, <div eID="gen31311" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen31312"/> <l level="1" sID="gen31313"/>Barbarus hic ego sum, quia non intelligor ulli,<l eID="gen31313" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen31314"/>I am a barbarian here, none understand me.<l eID="gen31314" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen31312"/> <div sID="gen31315" type="x-p"/> To speak in the church in an unknown tongue is to talk gibberish; it is to play the barbarian; it is to confound the audience, instead of instructing them; and for this reason is utterly vain and unprofitable. <div eID="gen31315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31316" type="x-p"/> II. Having thus established his point, in the two next verses he applies, 1. By advising them to be chiefly desirous of those gifts that were most for the church's edification, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.12">v. 12</reference>. "Forasmuch as you are zealous of spiritual gifts, this way it will become commendable zeal, be zealous to edify the church, to promote Christian knowledge and practice, and covet those gifts most that will do the best service to men's souls." This is the great rule he gives, which, 2. He applies to the matter in hand, that, if they did speak a foreign language, they should beg of God the gift of interpreting it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.13">v. 13</reference>. That these were different gifts, see <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.10">ch. xii. 10</reference>. Those might speak and understand a foreign language who could not readily translate it into their own: and yet was this necessary to the church's edification; for the church must understand, that it might be edified, which yet it could not do till the foreign language was translated into its own. Let him therefore pray for the gift of interpreting what he speaks in an unknown tongue; or rather covet and ask of God the gift of interpreting than of speaking in a language that needs interpretation, this being most for the church's benefit, and therefore among the gifts that excel; <hi type="italic">vide</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.12">v. 12</reference>. Some understand it, "Let him pray so as to interpret what he utters in prayer in a language unintelligible without it." The sum is that they should perform all religious exercises in their assemblies so that all might join in them and profit by them. 3. He enforces this advice with a proper reason, that, if <hi type="italic">he prayed in an unknown tongue, his spirit might pray,</hi> that is, a spiritual gift might be exercised in prayer, or his own mind might be devoutly engaged, <hi type="italic">but his understanding would be unfruitful</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.14">v. 14</reference>), that is, the sense and meaning of his words would be unfruitful, he would not be understood, nor therefore would others join with him in his devotions. Note, It should be the concern of such as pray in public to pray intelligibly, not in a foreign language, nor in a language that, if it be not foreign, is above the level of his audience. Language that is most obvious and easy to be understood is the most proper for public devotion and other religious exercises.
entries.9cea9a362979aecaff7ad0ac65c0c38139361855: <div eID="gen31316" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">On Spiritual Gifts. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31317" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also. <hi type="super">16</hi> Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest? <hi type="super">17</hi> For thou verily givest thanks well, but the other is not edified. <hi type="super">18</hi> I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all: <hi type="super">19</hi> Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that <hi type="italic">by my voice</hi> I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an <hi type="italic">unknown</hi> tongue. <hi type="super">20</hi> Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men. <div eID="gen31317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31318" type="x-p"/> The apostle here sums up the argument hitherto, and, <div eID="gen31318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31319" type="x-p"/> I. Directs them how they should sing and pray in public (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also. I will sing with the spirit,</hi> &c. He does not forbid their praying or singing under a divine <hi type="italic">afflatus,</hi> or when they were inspired for this purpose, or had such a spiritual gift communicated to them; but he would have them perform both so as to be understood by others, that others might join with them. Note, Public worship should be performed so as to be understood. <div eID="gen31319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31320" type="x-p"/> II. He enforces the argument with several reasons. <div eID="gen31320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31321" type="x-p"/> 1. That otherwise the unlearned could not say Amen to their prayers or thanksgivings, could not join in the worship, for they did not understand it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.16">v. 16</reference>. He who fills up or occupies the place of the unlearned, that is, as the ancients interpret it, the body of the people, who, in most Christian assemblies, are illiterate; how should they say <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> to prayers in an unknown tongue? How should they declare their consent and concurrence? This is saying <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> So be it. <hi type="italic">God grant the thing we have requested;</hi> or, We join in the confession that has been made of sin, and in the acknowledgment that has been made of divine mercies and favours. This is the import of saying <hi type="italic">Amen.</hi> All should say <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> inwardly; and it is not improper to testify this inward concurrence in public prayers and devotions, by an audible <hi type="italic">Amen.</hi> The ancient Christians said <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> aloud. <hi type="italic">Vide</hi> Just. Mart. <hi type="italic">apol.</hi> 2. <hi type="italic">prop&#232; fin.</hi> Now, how should the people say <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> to what they did not understand? Note, There can be no concurrence in those prayers that are not understood. The intention of public devotions is therefore entirely destroyed if they are performed in an unknown tongue. He who performs may pray well, and give thanks well, but not in that time and place, because others are not, cannot be, edified (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.17">v. 17</reference>) by what they understand not. <div eID="gen31321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31322" type="x-p"/> 2. He alleges his own example, to make the greater impression, concerning which observe, (1.) That he did not come behind any of them in this spiritual gift: "<hi type="italic">I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than you all</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.18">v. 18</reference>); not only more than any single person among you, but more than all together." It was not envy at their better furniture that made Paul depreciate what they so highly valued and so much vaunted of; he surpassed them all in this very gift of tongues, and did not vilify their gift because he had it not. This spirit of envy is too common in the world. But the apostle took care to guard against this misconstruction of his purpose, by letting them know there was more ground for them to envy him upon this head than for him to envy them. Note, When we beat down men's unreasonable value for themselves, or any of their possessions or attainments, we should let them see, if possible, that this does not proceed from an envious and grudging spirit. We miss our aim if they can fairly give our conduct this invidious turn. Paul could not be justly censured, nor suspected for any such principle in this whole argument. He spoke more language than they all. Yet, (2.) He had rather <hi type="italic">speak five words with understanding,</hi> that is, so as to be understood, and instruct and edify others, <hi type="italic">than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.19">v. 19</reference>. He was so far from valuing himself upon talking languages, or making ostentation of his talents of this kind, that he had rather speak five intelligible words, to benefit others, than make a thousand, ten thousand fine discourses, that would do no one else any good, because they did not understand them. Note, A truly Christian minister will value himself much more upon doing the least spiritual good to men's souls than upon procuring the greatest applause and commendation to himself. This is true grandeur and nobleness of spirit; it is acting up to his character; it is approving himself the servant of Christ, and not a vassal to his own pride and vanity. <div eID="gen31322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31323" type="x-p"/> 3. He adds a plain intimation that the fondness then discovered for this gift was but too plain an indication of the immaturity of their judgment: <hi type="italic">Brethren, be not children in understanding; in malice be you children, but in understanding be men,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.20">v. 20</reference>. Children are apt to be struck with novelty and strange appearances. They are taken with an outward show, without enquiring into the true nature and worth of things. Do not you act like them, and prefer noise and show to worth and substance; show a greater ripeness of judgment, and act a more manly part; be like children in nothing but an innocent and inoffensive disposition. A double rebuke is couched in this passage, both of their pride upon account of their gifts, and their arrogance and haughtiness towards each other, and the contests and quarrels proceeding from them. Note, Christians should be harmless and inoffensive as children, void of all guile and malice; but should have wisdom and knowledge that are ripe and mature. They should not be unskilful in the word of righteousness (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.13">Heb. v. 13</reference>), though they should be unskilful in all the arts of mischief.
entries.33eddbb621cb1d843555e480031678538525e046: <div eID="gen31323" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">On Spiritual Gifts. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31324" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> In the law it is written, With <hi type="italic">men of</hi> other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord. <hi type="super">22</hi> Wherefore tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not: but prophesying <hi type="italic">serveth</hi> not for them that believe not, but for them which believe. <hi type="super">23</hi> If therefore the whole church be come together into one place, and all speak with tongues, and there come in <hi type="italic">those that are</hi> unlearned, or unbelievers, will they not say that ye are mad? 24 But if all prophesy, and there come in one that believeth not, or <hi type="italic">one</hi> unlearned, he is convinced of all, he is judged of all: <hi type="super">25</hi> And thus are the secrets of his heart made manifest; and so falling down on <hi type="italic">his</hi> face he will worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth. <div eID="gen31324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31325" type="x-p"/> In this passage the apostle pursues the argument, and reasons from other topics; as, <div eID="gen31325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31326" type="x-p"/> I. Tongues, as the Corinthians used them, were rather a token of judgment from God than mercy to any people (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">In the law</hi> (that is, the Old Testament) <hi type="italic">it is written, With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak to this people; and yet for all this they will not hear me, saith the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.11">Isa. xxviii. 11</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.28.46">Deut. xxviii. 46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.49">49</reference>. To both these passages, it is thought, the apostle refers. Both are delivered by way of threatening, and one is supposed to interpret the other. The meaning in this view is that it is an evidence that a people are abandoned of God when he gives them up to this sort of instruction, to the discipline of those who speak in another language. And surely the apostle's discourse implies, "You should not be fond of the tokens of divine displeasure. God can have no gracious regards to those who are left merely to this sort of instruction, and taught in language which they cannot understand. They can never be benefited by such teaching as this; and, when they are left to it, it is a sad sign that God gives them over as past cure." And should Christians covet to be in such a state, or to bring the churches into it? Yet thus did the Corinthian preachers in effect, who would always deliver their inspirations in an unknown tongue. <div eID="gen31326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31327" type="x-p"/> II. Tongues were rather a sign to unbelievers than to believers, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.22">v. 22</reference>. They were a spiritual gift, intended for the conviction and conversion of infidels, that they might be brought into the Christian church; but converts were to be built up in Christianity by profitable instructions in their own language. The gift of tongues was necessary to spread Christianity, and gather churches; it was proper and intended to convince unbelievers of that doctrine which Christians had already embraced; but prophesying, and interpreting scripture in their own language, were most for the edification of such as did already believe: so that speaking with tongues in Christians assemblies was altogether out of time and place; neither one nor the other was proper for it. Note, That gifts may be rightly used, it is proper to know the ends which they are intended to serve. To go about the conversion of infidels, as the apostles did, had been a vain undertaking without the gift of tongues, and the discovery of this gift; but, in an assembly of Christians already converted to the Christian faith, to make use and ostentation of this gift would be perfectly impertinent, because it would be of no advantage to the assembly; not for conviction of truth, because they had already embraced it; not for their edification, because they did not understand, and could not get benefit without understanding, what they heard. <div eID="gen31327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31328" type="x-p"/> III. The credit and reputation of their assemblies among unbelievers required them to prefer prophesying before speaking with tongues. For, 1. If, when they were all assembled for Christian worship, their ministers, or all employed in public worship, should talk unintelligible language, and infidels should drop in, they would conclude them to be mad, to be no better than a parcel of wild fanatics. Who in their right senses could carry on religious worship in such a manner? Or what sort of religion is that which leaves out sense and understanding? Would not this make Christianity ridiculous to a heathen, to hear the ministers of it pray, or preach, or perform any other religious exercise, in a language that neither he nor the assembly understood? Note, The Christian religion is a sober and reasonable thing in itself, and should not, by the ministers of it, be made to look wild or senseless. Those disgrace their religion, and vilify their own character, who do any thing that has this aspect. But, on the other hand, 2. If, instead of speaking with tongues, those who minister plainly interpret scripture, or preach, in language intelligible and proper, the great truths and rules of the gospel, a heathen or unlearned person, coming in, will probably be convinced, and become a convert to Christianity (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.24-1Cor.14.25">v. 24, 25</reference>); his conscience will be touched, the secrets of his heart will be revealed to him, he will be condemned by the truth he hears, and so will be brought to confess his guilt, to pay his homage to God, and own that he is indeed among you, present in the assembly. Note, Scripture—truth, plainly and duly taught, has a marvellous aptness to awaken the conscience, and touch the heart. And is not this much more for the honour of our religion than that infidels should conclude the ministers of it a set of madmen, and their religious exercises only fits of frenzy? This last would at once cast contempt on them and their religion too. Instead of procuring applause for them, it would render them ridiculous, and involve their profession in the same censure: whereas prophesying would certainly edify the church, much better keep up their credit, and might probably convince and convert infidels who might occasionally hear them. Note, Religious exercises in Christian assemblies should be such as are fit to edify the faithful, and convince, affect, and convert unbelievers. The ministry was not instituted to make ostentation of gifts and parts, but to save souls.
entries.0c892610f118d8475bb776e68ac11d65de90c22b: <div eID="gen31328" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">On Spiritual Gifts. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31329" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying. <hi type="super">27</hi> If any man speak in an <hi type="italic">unknown</hi> tongue, <hi type="italic">let it be</hi> by two, or at the most <hi type="italic">by</hi> three, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> by course; and let one interpret. 28 But if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church; and let him speak to himself, and to God. <hi type="super">29</hi> Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge. <hi type="super">30</hi> If <hi type="italic">any thing</hi> be revealed to another that sitteth by, let the first hold his peace. <hi type="super">31</hi> For ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. <hi type="super">33</hi> For God is not <hi type="italic">the author</hi> of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints. <div eID="gen31329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31330" type="x-p"/> In this passage the apostle reproves them for their disorder, and endeavours to correct and regulate their conduct for the future. <div eID="gen31330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31331" type="x-p"/> I. He blames them for the confusion they introduced into the assembly, by ostentation of their gifts (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">When you come together every one hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue,</hi> &c.; that is, "You are apt to confound the several parts of worship; and, while one has a psalm to utter by inspiration, another has a doctrine, or revelation;" or else, "You are apt to be confused in the same branch of worship, many of you having psalms or doctrines to propose at the same time, without staying for one another. Is not this perfect uproar? Can this be edifying? And yet all religious exercises in public assemblies should have this view, <hi type="italic">Let all things be done to edifying.</hi>" <div eID="gen31331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31332" type="x-p"/> II. He corrects their faults, and lays down some regulations for their future conduct. 1. As to speaking in an unknown tongue, he orders that no more than two or three should do it at one meeting, and this not altogether, but successively, one after another. And even this was not to be done unless there were some one to interpret (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.27-1Cor.14.28">v. 27, 28</reference>), some other interpreter besides himself, who spoke; for to speak in an unknown tongue what he himself was afterwards to interpret could only be for ostentation. But, if another were present who could interpret, two miraculous gifts might be exercised at once, and thereby the church edified, and the faith of the hearers confirmed at the same time. But, if there were none to interpret, he was to be silent in the church, and only exercise his gift between God and himself (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.28">v. 28</reference>), that is (as I think) in private, at home; for all who are present at public worship should join in it, and not be at their private devotions in public assemblies. Solitary devotions are out of time and place when the church has met for social worship. 2. As to prophesying he orders, (1.) That two or three only should speak at one meeting (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.20">v. 20</reference>), and this successively, not all at once; and that the other should examine and judge what he delivered, that is, discern and determine concerning it, whether it were of divine inspiration or not. There might be false prophets, mere pretenders to divine inspiration; and the true prophets were to judge of these, and discern and discover who was divinely inspired, and by such inspiration interpreted scripture, and taught the church, and who was not—what was of divine inspiration and what was not. This seems to be the meaning of this rule. For where a prophet was known to be such, and under the divine <hi type="italic">afflatus,</hi> he could not be judged; for this were to subject even the Holy Spirit to the judgment of men. He who was indeed inspired, and known to be so, was above all human judgment. (2.) He orders that, if any assistant prophet had a revelation, while another was prophesying, the other should hold his peace, be silent (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.30">v. 30</reference>), before the inspired assistant uttered his revelation. Indeed, it is by many understood that the former speaker should immediately hold his peace. But this seems unnatural, and not so well to agree with the context. For why must one that was speaking by inspiration be immediately silent upon another man's being inspired, and suppress what was dictated to him by the same Spirit? Indeed, he who had the new revelation might claim liberty of speech in his turn, upon producing his vouchers; but why must liberty of speech be taken from him who was speaking before, and his mouth stopped, when he was delivering the dictates of the same Spirit, and could produce the same vouchers? Would the Spirit of God move one to speak, and, before he had delivered what he had to say, move another to interrupt him, and put him to silence? This seems to me an unnatural thought. Nor is it more agreeable to the context, and the reason annexed (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">That all might prophesy, one by one,</hi> or one after another, which could not be where any one was interrupted and silenced before he had done prophesying; but might easily be if he who was afterwards inspired forbore to deliver his new revelation till the former prophet had finished what he had to say. And, to confirm this sense, the apostle quickly adds, <hi type="italic">The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.33">v. 33</reference>); that is, the spiritual gifts they have leave them still possessed of their reason, and capable of using their own judgment in the exercise of them. Divine inspirations are not, like the diabolical possessions of heathen priests, violent and ungovernable, and prompting them to act as if they were beside themselves; but are sober and calm, and capable of regular conduct. The man inspired by the Spirit of God may still act the man, and observe the rules of natural order and decency in delivering his revelations. His spiritual gift is thus far subject to his pleasure, and to be managed by his discretion. <div eID="gen31332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31333" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle gives the reasons of these regulations. As, 1. That they would be for the church's benefit, their instruction and consolation. It is that <hi type="italic">all may learn, and all may be comforted or exhorted,</hi> that the prophets were to speak in the orderly manner the apostle advises. Note, The instruction, edification, and comfort of the church, is that for which God instituted the ministry. And surely ministers should, as much as possible, fit their ministrations to these purposes. 2. He tells them, <hi type="italic">God is not the God of confusion, but of peace and good order,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.33">v. 33</reference>. Therefore divine inspiration should by no means throw Christian assemblies into confusion, and break through all rules of common decency, which yet would be unavoidable if several inspired men should all at once utter what was suggested to them by the Spirit of God, and not wait to take their turns. Note, The honour of God requires that things should be managed in Christian assemblies so as not to transgress the rules of natural decency. If they are managed in a tumultuous and confused manner, what a notion must this give of the God who is worshipped, to considerate observers! Does it look as if he were the God of peace and order, and an enemy to confusion? Things should be managed so in divine worship that no unlovely nor dishonourable notion of God should be formed in the minds of observers. 3. He adds that things were thus orderly managed in all the other churches: <hi type="italic">As in all the churches of the saints</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.33">v. 33</reference>); they kept to these rules in the exercise of their spiritual gifts, which was a manifest proof that the church of Corinth might observe the same regulations. And it would be perfectly scandalous for them, who exceeded most churches in spiritual gifts, to be more disorderly than any in the exercise of them. Note, Though other churches are not to be our rule, yet the regard they pay to the rules of natural decency and order should restrain us from breaking these rules. Thus far they may be proposed as examples, and it is a shame not to follow them.
entries.9731bc5bf08e4b68f3564a2baa8edfc4464a94ca: <div eID="gen31333" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">On Spiritual Gifts. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31334" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">34</hi> Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but <hi type="italic">they are commanded</hi> to be under obedience, as also saith the law. <hi type="super">35</hi> And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home: for it is a shame for women to speak in the church. <div eID="gen31334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31335" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle, 1. Enjoins silence on their women in public assemblies, and to such a degree that they must not ask questions for their own information in the church, but ask their husbands at home. <hi type="italic">They are to learn in silence with all subjection; but,</hi> says the apostle, <hi type="italic">I suffer them not to teach,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11-1Tim.2.12">1 Tim. ii. 11, 12</reference>. There is indeed an intimation (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.5">ch. xi. 5</reference>) as if the women sometimes did pray and prophecy in their assemblies, which the apostle, in that passage, does not simply condemn, but the manner of performance, that is, praying or prophesying with the head uncovered, which, in that age and country, was throwing off the distinction of sexes, and setting themselves on a level with the men. But here he seems to forbid all public performances of theirs. They are not permitted to speak (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">v. 34</reference>) in the church, neither in praying nor prophesying. The connection seems plainly to include the latter, in the limited sense in which it is taken in this chapter, namely, for preaching, or interpreting scripture by inspiration. And, indeed, for a woman to prophesy in this sense were to teach, which does not so well befit her state of subjection. A teacher of others has in that respect a superiority over them, which is not allowed the woman over the man, nor must she therefore be allowed to teach in a congregation: <hi type="italic">I suffer them not to teach.</hi> But praying, and uttering hymns inspired, were not teaching. And seeing there were women who had spiritual gifts of this sort in that age of the church (see <reference osisRef="Acts.22.9">Acts xxii. 9</reference>), and might be under this impulse in the assembly, must they altogether suppress it? Or why should they have this gift, if it must never be publicly exercised? For these reasons, some think that these general prohibitions are only to be understood in common cases; but that upon extraordinary occasions, when women were under a divine <hi type="italic">afflatus,</hi> and known to be so, they might have liberty of speech. They were not ordinarily to teach, nor so much as to debate and ask questions in the church, but learn in silence there; and, if difficulties occurred, <hi type="italic">ask their own husbands at home.</hi> Note, As it is the woman's duty to learn in subjection, it is the man's duty to keep up his superiority, by being able to instruct her; if it be her duty to ask her husband at home, it is his concern and duty to endeavour at lest to be able to answer her enquiries; if it be a shame for her to speak in the church, where she should be silent, it is a shame for him to be silent when he should speak, and not be able to give an answer, when she asks him at home. 2. We have here the reason of this injunction: It is God's law and commandment that they should be under obedience (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">v. 34</reference>); they are placed in subordination to the man, and it is a shame for them to do any thing that looks like an affectation of changing ranks, which speaking in public seemed to imply, at least in that age, and among that people, as would public teaching much more: so that the apostle concludes it was a shame for women to speak in the church, in the assembly. Shame is the mind's uneasy reflection on having done an indecent thing. And what more indecent than for a woman to quit her rank, renounce the subordination of her sex, or do what in common account had such aspect and appearance? Note, Our spirit and conduct should be suitable to our rank. The natural distinctions God has made, we should observe. Those he has placed in subjection to others should not set themselves on a level, nor affect or assume superiority. The woman was made subject to the man, and she should keep her station and be content with it. For this reason women must be silent in the churches, not set up for teachers; for this is setting up for superiority over the man.
entries.046515c6146922482be0d6d99e7c4e0ac0301992: <div eID="gen31335" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">On Spiritual Gifts. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31336" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> What? came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only? <hi type="super">37</hi> If any man think himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord. <hi type="super">38</hi> But if any man be ignorant, let him be ignorant. <hi type="super">39</hi> Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues. 40 Let all things be done decently and in order. <div eID="gen31336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31337" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle closes his argument, 1. With a just rebuke of the Corinthians for their extravagant pride and self-conceit: they so managed with their spiritual gifts as no church did like them; they behaved in a manner by themselves, and would not easily endure control nor regulation. Now, says the apostle, to beat down this arrogant humour, "<hi type="italic">Came the gospel out from you? Or came it to you only?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.36">v. 36</reference>. Did Christianity come our of Corinth? was its original among you? Or, if not, is it now limited and confined to you? are you the only church favoured with divine revelations, that you will depart from the decent usages of all other churches, and, to make ostentation of your spiritual gifts, bring confusion into Christian assemblies? How intolerably assuming is this behaviour! Pray bethink yourselves." When it was needful or proper the apostle could rebuke with all authority; and surely his rebukes, if ever, were proper here. Note, Those must be reproved and humbled whose spiritual pride and self-conceit throw Christian churches and assemblies into confusion, though such men will hardly bear even the rebukes of an apostle. 2. He lets them know that what he said to them was the command of God; nor durst any true prophet, any one really inspired, deny it (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.37">v. 37</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If any man think himself a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge,</hi> &c., nay, let him be tried by this very rule. If he will not own what I deliver on this head to be the will of Christ, he himself never had the Spirit of Christ. The Spirit of Christ can never contradict itself; if it speak in me, and in them, it must speak the same things in both. If their revelations contradict mine, they do not come from the same Spirit; either I or they must be false prophets. <hi type="italic">By this therefore you may know them.</hi> If they say that my directions in this matter are no divine commandments, you may depend upon it they are not divinely inspired. But if any continue after all, through prejudice or obstinacy, uncertain or ignorant whether they or I speak by the Spirit of God, they must be left under the power of this ignorance. If their pretences to inspiration can stand in competition with the apostolical character and powers which I have, I have lost all my authority and influence; and the persons who allow of this competition against me are out of the reach of conviction, and must be left to themselves." Note, It is just with God to leave those to the blindness of their own minds who wilfully shut out the light. Those who would be ignorant in so plain a case were justly left under the power of their mistake. 3. He sums up all in two general advices:—(1.) That though they should not despise the gift of tongues, nor altogether disuse it, under the regulations mentioned, yet they should prefer prophesying. This is indeed the scope of the whole argument. It was to be preferred to the other, because it was the more useful gift. (2.) He charges them to let all things be done decently and in order (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.40">v. 40</reference>), that is, that they should avoid every thing that was manifestly indecent and disorderly. Not that they should hence take occasion to bring into the Christian church and worship any thing that a vain mind might think ornamental to it, or that would help to set it off. Such indecencies and disorders as he had remarked upon were especially to be shunned. They must do nothing that was manifestly childish (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.20">v. 20</reference>), or that would give occasion to say they were mad (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.23">v. 23</reference>), nor must they act so as to breed confusion, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.33">v. 33</reference>. This would be utterly indecent; it would make a tumult and mob of a Christian assembly. But they were to do things in order; they were to speak one after another, and not all at once; take their turns, and not interrupt one another. To do otherwise was to destroy the end of a Christians ministry, and all assemblies for Christian worship. Note, Manifest indecencies and disorders are to be carefully kept out of all Christian churches, and every part of divine worship. They should have nothing in them that is childish, absurd, ridiculous, wild, or tumultuous; but all parts of divine worship should be carried on in a manly, grave, rational, composed, and orderly manner. God is not to be dishonoured, nor his worship disgraced, by our unbecoming and disorderly performance of it and attendance at it.  <chapter eID="1Cor.14"/> <div eID="gen31337" type="x-p"/>

entries.dcf54caa034bd0d6bf929373b4b73cb6d4668485: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17048"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <div sID="gen33750" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1-1Cor.14.25">1Co 14:1-25</reference>. Superiority of Prophecy over Tongues.<div eID="gen33750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17048"/><hi type="bold">1. Follow after charity--</hi>as your first and chief aim, seeing that it is "the greatest" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.13">1Co 13:13</reference>).<div eID="gen33751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and desire--</hi>Translate, "Yet (as a secondary aim) desire zealously (see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.31">1Co 12:31</reference>) spiritual gifts."<div eID="gen33752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but rather--</hi>"but chiefly that ye may prophesy" (speak and exhort under inspiration) (<reference osisRef="Prov.29.18">Pr 29:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.1">Ac 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.20">1Th 5:20</reference>), whether as to future events, that is, strict prophecy, or explaining obscure parts of Scripture, especially the prophetical Scriptures or illustrating and setting forth questions of Christian doctrine and practice. Our modern preaching is the successor of prophecy, but without the inspiration. Desire zealously this (prophecy) more than any other spiritual gift; or in preference to "tongues" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.2">1Co 14:2</reference>, &c.) [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33753" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a68dcaab30baab476cda00c7ea1920a9d5b5fd7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17049"/><div sID="gen33754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17049"/><hi type="bold">2. speaketh ... unto God--</hi>who alone understands all languages.<div eID="gen33754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no man understandeth--</hi>generally speaking; the few who have the gift of interpreting tongues are the exception.<div eID="gen33755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the spirit--</hi>as opposed to "the understanding" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.14">1Co 14:14</reference>).<div eID="gen33756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mysteries--</hi>unintelligible to the hearers, exciting their wonder, rather than instructing them. Corinth, being a mart resorted to by merchants from Asia, Africa, and Europe, would give scope amidst its mixed population for the exercise of the gift of tongues; but its legitimate use was in an audience understanding the tongue of the speaker, not, as the Corinthians abused it, in mere display. <div eID="gen33757" type="x-p"/>
entries.232612fb1d50edee96319eee3949c69e84599d7c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17050"/><div sID="gen33758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17050"/><hi type="bold">3. But--</hi>on the other hand.<div eID="gen33758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">edification--</hi>of which the two principal species given are "exhortation" to remove sluggishness, "comfort" or consolation to remove sadness [Bengel]. Omit "to." <div eID="gen33759" type="x-p"/>
entries.6382077ac6c383e6ce8351fd485c58ae4fbe9c47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17051"/><div sID="gen33760" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17051"/><hi type="bold">4. edifieth himself--</hi>as he understands the meaning of what the particular "tongue" expresses; but "the church," that is, the congregation, does not. <div eID="gen33760" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ea0f43f740d26880ae4db07596c527899134ca7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17052"/><div sID="gen33761" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17052"/>5. Translate, "Now I wish you all to speak with tongues (so far am I from thus speaking through having any objection to tongues), but rather IN ORDER THAT (as my ulterior and higher wish for you) ye should prophesy." Tongues must therefore mean languages, not ecstatic, unintelligible rhapsodie (as Neander fancied): for Paul could never "wish" for the latter in their behalf.<div eID="gen33761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">greater--</hi>because more useful.<div eID="gen33762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33763" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">except he interpret--</hi>the unknown tongue which he speaks, "that the Church may receive edifying (building up)." <div eID="gen33763" type="x-p"/>
entries.d115c335c24cdea8656b46e75415c8d59e63ef72: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17053"/><div sID="gen33764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17053"/>6. Translate, "But now"; seeing there is no edification without interpretation.<div eID="gen33764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">revelation ... prophesying--</hi>corresponding one to the other; "revelation" being the supernatural unveiling of divine truths to man, "prophesying" the enunciation to men of such revelations. So "knowledge" corresponds to "doctrine," which is the gift of teaching to others our knowledge. As the former pair refers to specially revealed mysteries, so the latter pair refers to the general obvious truths of salvation, brought from the common storehouse of believers. <div eID="gen33765" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d635e304e848a61c2cce4fa9a4f7de446c78324: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17054"/><div sID="gen33766" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17054"/>7. Translate, "And things without life-giving sound, whether pipe or harp, YET (notwithstanding their giving sound) if they give not a distinction in the tones (that is, notes) how?" &c.<div eID="gen33766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what is piped or harped--</hi>that is, what tune is played on the pipe or harp. <div eID="gen33767" type="x-p"/>
entries.1fdf0a8686b1e806e82578de2f0f3af3a51bab19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17055"/><div sID="gen33768" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17055"/>8. Translate, "For if also," an additional step in the argument.<div eID="gen33768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncertain sound--</hi>having no definite meaning: whereas it ought to be so marked that one succession of notes on the trumpet should summon the soldiers to attack; another, to retreat; another, to some other evolution. <div eID="gen33769" type="x-p"/>
entries.56c20d22e35e6c57609fa609d98a3784c8bfc956: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17056"/><div sID="gen33770" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17056"/><hi type="bold">9. So ... ye--</hi>who have life; as opposed to "things without life" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.7">1Co 14:7</reference>).<div eID="gen33770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the tongue--</hi>the language which ye speak in.<div eID="gen33771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye shall speak--</hi>Ye will be speaking into the air, that is, in vain (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.26">1Co 9:26</reference>). <div eID="gen33772" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e1fdf157be15a31fe2ea1022a0723a5f47293e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17057"/><div sID="gen33773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17057"/><hi type="bold">10. it may be--</hi>that is, perhaps, speaking by conjecture. "It may chance" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.37">1Co 15:37</reference>).<div eID="gen33773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so many--</hi>as may be enumerated by investigators of such matters. Compare "so much," used generally for a definite number left undefined (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.8">Ac 5:8</reference>; also <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.8">2Sa 12:8</reference>).<div eID="gen33774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kinds of voices--</hi>kinds of articulate speech.<div eID="gen33775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without signification--</hi>without articulate voice (that is, distinct meaning). None is without its own voice, or mode of speech, distinct from the rest. <div eID="gen33776" type="x-p"/>
entries.914fb9501061663fd7d4a354ce107f53442aa5b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17058"/><div sID="gen33777" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17058"/><hi type="bold">11. Therefore--</hi>seeing that none is without meaning.<div eID="gen33777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a barbarian--</hi>a foreigner (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.2">Ac 28:2</reference>). Not in the depreciatory sense as the term is now used, but one speaking a foreign language. <div eID="gen33778" type="x-p"/>
entries.6413c866056d34ded6c460c02f2380b8bd5854a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17059"/><div sID="gen33779" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17059"/><hi type="bold">12. zealous--</hi>emulously desirous.<div eID="gen33779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spiritual gifts--</hi>literally, "spirits"; that is, emanations from the one Spirit.<div eID="gen33780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek that ye may excel to--</hi>Translate, "Seek them, that ye may abound in them to the edifying," &c. <div eID="gen33781" type="x-p"/>
entries.26a224f52f8d7fb25e1ad742e1959b88368a294a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17060"/><div sID="gen33782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17060"/>13. Explain, "Let him who speaketh with a tongue [unknown] in his prayer (or, when praying) strive that he may interpret" [Alford]. This explanation of "pray" is needed by its logical connection with "prayer in an unknown tongue" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.14">1Co 14:14</reference>). Though his words be unintelligible to his hearers, let him in them pray that he may obtain the gift of interpreting, which will make them "edifying" to "the church" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.12">1Co 14:12</reference>). <div eID="gen33782" type="x-p"/>
entries.074935eae722f3f1783cb2c9f0eb932b2d9f474d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17061"/><div sID="gen33783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17061"/><hi type="bold">14. spirit--</hi>my higher being, the passive object of the Holy Spirit's operations, and the instrument of prayer in the unknown tongue, distinguished from the "understanding," the active instrument of thought and reasoning; which in this case must be "unfruitful" in edifying others, since the vehicle of expression is unintelligible to them. On the distinction of soul or mind and spirit, see <reference osisRef="Eph.4.23">Ep 4:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">He 4:12</reference>. <div eID="gen33783" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fd126a5896f131fcdd8c64986fb4ffee8bde1a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17062"/><div sID="gen33784" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17062"/><hi type="bold">15. What is it then?--</hi>What is my determination thereupon?<div eID="gen33784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>rather as Greek, "but"; I will not only pray with my spirit, which (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.14">1Co 14:14</reference>) might leave the understanding unedified, BUT with the understanding also [Alford and Ellicott].<div eID="gen33785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pray with the understanding also--</hi>and, by inference, I will keep silence altogether if I cannot pray with the understanding (so as to make myself understood by others). A prescient warning, mutatis mutandis, against the Roman and Greek practice of keeping liturgies in dead languages, which long since have become unintelligible to the masses; though their forefathers spoke them at a time when those liturgies were framed for general use. <div eID="gen33786" type="x-p"/>
entries.945597deeaa10aec9b26ddf6391b8330eb97e4ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17063"/><div sID="gen33787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17063"/><hi type="bold">16. Else ... thou--</hi>He changes from the first person, as he had just expressed his own resolution, "I will pray with the understanding," whatever "thou" doest.<div eID="gen33787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bless--</hi>the highest kind of prayer.<div eID="gen33788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">occupieth the room of the unlearned--</hi>one who, whatever other gifts he may possess, yet, as wanting the gift of interpretation, is reduced by the speaking in an unknown tongue to the position of one unlearned, or "a private person."<div eID="gen33789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">say Amen--</hi>Prayer is not a vicarious duty done by others for us; as in Rome's liturgies and masses. We must join with the leader of the prayers and praises of the congregation, and say aloud our responsive "Amen" in assent, as was the usage of the Jewish (<reference osisRef="Deut.27.15-Deut.27.26">De 27:15-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.8.6">Ne 8:6</reference>) and Christian primitive churches [Justin Martyr, Apology, 2. 97]. <div eID="gen33790" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fa88a603f5ccc2099460aaa049993601c48e197: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17064"/><div sID="gen33791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17064"/><hi type="bold">17. givest thanks--</hi>The prayers of the synagogue were called "eulogies," because to each prayer was joined a thanksgiving. Hence the prayers of the Christian Church also were called blessings and giving of thanks. This illustrates <reference osisRef="Col.4.2">Col 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.17">1Th 5:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.18">18</reference>. So the Kaddisch and Keduscha, the synagogue formulæ of "hallowing" the divine "name" and of prayer for the "coming of God's kingdom," answer to the Church's Lord's Prayer, repeated often and made the foundation on which the other prayers are built [Tertullian, Prayer]. <div eID="gen33791" type="x-p"/>
entries.96404d7e786d03920fbab69fc531a1b5d9addaed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17065"/><div sID="gen33792" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17065"/><hi type="bold">18. tongues--</hi>The oldest manuscripts have the singular, "in a tongue [foreign]." <div eID="gen33792" type="x-p"/>
entries.5156f965ce5befd402f425fe219f43ded08b1c8f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17066"/><div sID="gen33793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17066"/><hi type="bold">19. I had rather--</hi>The Greek verb more literally expresses this meaning, "I WISH to speak five words with my understanding (rather) than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue"; even the two thousandth part of ten thousand. The Greek for "I would rather," would be a different verb. Paul would NOT wish at all to speak "ten thousand words in an unknown tongue." <div eID="gen33793" type="x-p"/>
entries.823573a8bf76c5930fae94973cbc3b7871dd1267: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17067"/><div sID="gen33794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17067"/><hi type="bold">20. Brethren--</hi>an appellation calculated to conciliate their favorable reception of his exhortation.<div eID="gen33794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children in understanding--</hi>as preference of gifts abused to nonedification would make you (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">1Co 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">Mt 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.19">Ro 16:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Ep 4:14</reference>). The Greek for "understanding" expresses the will of one's spirit, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.6">Ro 8:6</reference> (it is not found elsewhere); as the "heart" is the will of the "soul." The same Greek is used for "minded" in <reference osisRef="Rom.8.6">Ro 8:6</reference>.<div eID="gen33795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men--</hi>full-grown. Be childlike, not childish. <div eID="gen33796" type="x-p"/>
entries.8de0b1c1d6455591bea8a29e7a6bef02d4580247: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17068"/><div sID="gen33797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17068"/><hi type="bold">21. In the law--</hi>as the whole Old Testament is called, being all of it the law of God. Compare the citation of the Psalms as the "law," <reference osisRef="John.10.34">Joh 10:34</reference>. Here the quotation is from <reference osisRef="Isa.28.11">Is 28:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.12">12</reference>, where God virtually says of Israel, This people hear Me not, though I speak to. them in the language with which they are familiar; I will therefore speak to them in other tongues, namely, those of the foes whom I will send against them; but even then they will not hearken to Me; which Paul thus applies, Ye see that it is a penalty to be associated with men of a strange tongue, yet ye impose this on the Church [Grotius]; they who speak in foreign tongues are like "children" just "weaned from the milk" (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.9">Is 28:9</reference>), "with stammering lips" speaking unintelligibly to the hearers, appearing ridiculous (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.14">Is 28:14</reference>), or as babbling drunkards (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.13">Ac 2:13</reference>), or madmen (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.23">1Co 14:23</reference>). <div eID="gen33797" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e15b3a7121764509c40dae544ca30c29847749f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17069"/><div sID="gen33798" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17069"/>22. Thus from Isaiah it appears, reasons Paul, that "tongues" (unknown and uninterpreted) are not a sign mainly intended for believers (though at the conversion of Cornelius and the Gentiles with him, tongues were vouchsafed to him and them to confirm their faith), but mainly to be a condemnation to those, the majority, who, like Israel in Isaiah's day, reject the sign and the accompanying message. Compare "yet ... will they not hear Me" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.21">1Co 14:21</reference>). "Sign" is often used for a condemnatory sign (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.3">Eze 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.39-Matt.12.42">Mt 12:39-42</reference>). Since they will not understand, they shall not understand.<div eID="gen33798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prophesying ... not for them that believe not, but ... believe--</hi>that is, prophesying has no effect on them that are radically and obstinately like Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.11">Is 28:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.12">12</reference>), unbelievers, but on them that are either in receptivity or in fact believers; it makes believers of those not wilfully unbelievers (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.24">1Co 14:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.17">Ro 10:17</reference>), and spiritually nourishes those that already believe. <div eID="gen33799" type="x-p"/>
entries.5532d14114c2ff138c8f096be0e11d2d56072652: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17070"/><div sID="gen33800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17070"/><hi type="bold">23. whole ... all ... tongues--</hi>The more there are assembled, and the more that speak in unknown tongues, the more will the impression be conveyed to strangers "coming in" from curiosity ("unbelievers"), or even from a better motive ("unlearned"), that the whole body of worshippers is a mob of fanatical "madmen"; and that "the Church is like the company of builders of Babel after the confusion of tongues, or like the cause tried between two deaf men before a deaf judge, celebrated in the Greek epigram" [Grotius].<div eID="gen33800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unlearned--</hi>having some degree of faith, but not gifts [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33801" type="x-p"/>
entries.4cbb9a7bd1949364c02f8a95092102aa6e6e6540: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17071"/><div sID="gen33802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17071"/><hi type="bold">24. all--</hi>one by one (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.31">1Co 14:31</reference>).<div eID="gen33802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prophesy--</hi>speak the truth by the Spirit intelligibly, and not in unintelligible tongues.<div eID="gen33803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one--</hi>"anyone." Here singular; implying that this effect, namely, conviction by all, would be produced on anyone, who might happen to enter. In <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.23">1Co 14:23</reference> the plural is used; "unlearned or unbelievers"; implying that however many there might be, not one would profit by the tongues; yea, their being many would confirm them in rejecting the sign, as many unbelieving men together strengthen one another in unbelief; individuals are more easily won [Bengel].<div eID="gen33804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">convinced--</hi>convicted in conscience; said of the "one that believeth not" (<reference osisRef="John.16.8">Joh 16:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.16.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen33805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judged--</hi>His secret character is opened out. "Is searched into" [Alford]. Said of the "one unlearned" (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.15">1Co 2:15</reference>). <div eID="gen33806" type="x-p"/>
entries.d76097a3c894933eeec3dcd4f967172193951dc1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17072"/><div sID="gen33807" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17072"/><hi type="bold">25. And thus--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts and versions.<div eID="gen33807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">secrets of his heart made manifest--</hi>He sees his own inner character opened out by the sword of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">He 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.23">Jas 1:23</reference>), the word of God, in the hand of him who prophesieth. Compare the same effect produced on Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.30">Da 2:30</reference> and end of <reference osisRef="Dan.2.47">Da 2:47</reference>). No argument is stronger for the truth of religion than its manifestation of men to themselves in their true character. Hence hearers even now often think the preacher must have aimed his sermon particularly at them.<div eID="gen33808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and so--</hi>convicted at last, judged, and manifested to himself. Compare the effect on the woman of Samaria produced by Jesus' unfolding of her character to herself (<reference osisRef="John.4.19">Joh 4:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.4.29">29</reference>).<div eID="gen33809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and report--</hi>to his friends at home, as the woman of Samaria did. Rather, as the Greek is, "He will worship God, announcing," that is, openly avowing then and there, "that God is in you of a truth," and by implication that the God who is in you is of a truth the God.<div eID="gen33810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33811" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.26-1Cor.14.40">1Co 14:26-40</reference>. Rules for the Exercise of Gifts in the Congregation. <div eID="gen33811" type="x-p"/>
entries.8465b55a68e5bc51263e7a3d3ec7fa2f4504dfc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17073"/><div sID="gen33812" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17073"/><hi type="bold">26. How is it then?--</hi>rather, "What then is the true rule to be observed as to the use of gifts?" Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.15">1Co 14:15</reference>, where the same Greek occurs.<div eID="gen33812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a psalm--</hi>extemporary, inspired by the Spirit, as that of Mary, Zechariah, Simeon, and Anna (Lu 1:46-55, 67-79; 2:34-38).<div eID="gen33813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a doctrine--</hi>to impart and set forth to the congregation.<div eID="gen33814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a tongue ... a revelation--</hi>The oldest manuscripts transpose the order: "revelation ... tongue"; "interpretation" properly following "tongue" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.13">1Co 14:13</reference>).<div eID="gen33815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Let all things be done unto edifying--</hi>The general rule under which this particular case fails; an answer to the question at the beginning of this verse. Each is bound to obey the ordinances of his church not adverse to Scripture. See Article XXXIV, Church of England Prayer Book. <div eID="gen33816" type="x-p"/>
entries.0028a16251d710a2a38eeda24d458f35837332a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17074"/><div sID="gen33817" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17074"/><hi type="bold">27. let it be by two--</hi>at each time, in one assembly; not more than two or three might speak with tongues at each meeting.<div eID="gen33817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by course--</hi>in turns.<div eID="gen33818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33819" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let one interpret--</hi>one who has the gift of interpreting tongues; and not more than one. <div eID="gen33819" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e461a134cfa0a956542c4782e442b1efadd5693: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17075"/><div sID="gen33820" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17075"/><hi type="bold">28. let him--</hi>the speaker in unknown tongues.<div eID="gen33820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speak to himself, and to God--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.2">1Co 14:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.4">4</reference>)--privately and not in the hearing of others. <div eID="gen33821" type="x-p"/>
entries.079bbce9c9f0bb5a53593d8aec7e7ff3515c209d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17076"/><div sID="gen33822" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17076"/><hi type="bold">29. two or three--</hi>at one meeting (he does not add "at the most," as in <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.27">1Co 14:27</reference>, lest he should seem to "quench prophesyings," the most edifying of gifts), and these "one by one," in turn (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.27">1Co 14:27</reference>, "by course," and <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.31">1Co 14:31</reference>). Paul gives here similar rules to the prophets, as previously to those speaking in unknown tongues.<div eID="gen33822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33823" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judge--</hi>by their power of "discerning spirits" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.10">1Co 12:10</reference>), whether the person prophesying was really speaking under the influence of the Spirit (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1Co 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.13">1Jo 4:13</reference>). <div eID="gen33823" type="x-p"/>
entries.8505060177a52fe87dffd583fe40bc3673c5c9f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17077"/><div sID="gen33824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17077"/><hi type="bold">30. If any thing--</hi>Translate, "But if any thing."<div eID="gen33824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">another that sitteth by--</hi>a hearer.<div eID="gen33825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let the first hold his peace--</hi>Let him who heretofore spoke, and who came to the assembly furnished with a previous ordinary (in those times) revelation from God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.26">1Co 14:26</reference>), give place to him who at the assembly is moved to prophesy by a sudden revelation from the Spirit. <div eID="gen33826" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a884442c20fece2fd0f0f15ac89ac3593dcd3eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17078"/><div sID="gen33827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17078"/><hi type="bold">31.
