When he says, <hi type="italic">husbands, </hi>he does not prohibit them from consulting the Prophets themselves, if necessary. For all husbands are not competent to give an answer in such a case; but, as he is reasoning here as to external polity, he reckons it sufficient to point out what is unseemly, that the Corinthians may guard against it. In the meantime, it is the part of the prudent reader to consider, that the things of which he here treats are intermediate and indifferent, in which there is nothing unlawful, but what is at variance with propriety and edification.<div eID="gen119879" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.14.35" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119878" osisID="1Cor.14.35" type="section"/>
entries.510d3e88b897b3113596897bff402504b7b8c5fa: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.14.36" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.14.36" sID="gen119880" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119881" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">36</hi> <hi type="italic"> Did the word of God come out from you?</hi> This is a somewhat sharper reproof, but nothing more than was needful for beating down the haughtiness of the Corinthians. They were, beyond measure, self-complacent. They could not endure that either themselves, or what belonged to them, should be found fault with in anything. He asks, accordingly, whether they are the only Christians in the world; nay, farther, whether they are the first, or are to be the last? <hi type="italic">“Did the word of God,”</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">“come out from you?” </hi>that is, <hi type="italic">“Did </hi>it originate with you<hi type="italic">?” “Has </hi>it ended with you?” that is, <hi type="italic">“Will </hi>it spread no farther<hi type="italic">?” </hi>The design of the admonition is this — that they may not, without having any regard to others, please themselves in their own contrivances or customs. And this is a doctrine of general application; for no Church should be taken up with itself exclusively, to the neglect of others; but on the contrary, they ought all, in their turn, to hold out the right hand to each other, in the way of cherishing mutual fellowship, and accommodating themselves to each other, in so far as a regard to harmony requires. <note n="883"> <div sID="gen119882" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Autant qu’il est requis pour nourrir paix et concorde</foreign>;” — “in so far as it is requisite for maintaining peace and harmony.”<div eID="gen119882" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119883" type="x-p"/>But here it is asked, whether every Church, according as it has had the precedence of another in the order of time, <note n="884"> <div sID="gen119884" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et est plus ancienne</foreign>;” — “And is more ancient.”<div eID="gen119884" type="x-p"/> </note> has it also in its power to bind it to observe its institutions. <note n="885"> <div sID="gen119885" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A ses ordonnances et manieres de faire</foreign>;” — “To its ordinances and methods of acting.”<div eID="gen119885" type="x-p"/> </note> For Paul seems to intimate this in what he says. For example, Jerusalem was the mother of all the Churches, inasmuch as <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord had come out from it</hi> Was she then at liberty to assume to herself a superior right, so as to bind all others to follow her? I answer, that Paul here does not employ an argument of universal application, but one that was specially applicable to the Corinthians, as is frequently the case. He had, therefore, an eye to individuals, rather than to the thing itself. Hence it does not necessarily follow, that Churches that are of later origin must be bound to observe, in every point, the institutions of the earlier ones, inasmuch as even Paul himself did not bind himself by this rule, so as to obtrude upon other Churches the customs that were in use at Jerusalem. Let there be nothing of ambition — let there be nothing of obstinacy — let there be nothing of pride and contempt for other Churches — let there be, on the other hand, a desire to edify — let there be moderation and prudence; and in that case, amidst a diversity of observances, there will be nothing that is worthy of reproof.<div eID="gen119883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119886" type="x-p"/>Let us, therefore, bear in mind, that the haughtiness of the Corinthians is here reproved, who, concerned for themselves exclusively, <note n="886"> <div sID="gen119887" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ne regardans qu’a eux mesmes, et se plaisans en leur facons de faire</foreign>;” — “Looking only to themselves, and pleasing themselves in their modes of acting.”<div eID="gen119887" type="x-p"/> </note> showed no respect to the Churches of earlier origin, from which they had received the gospel, and did not endeavor to accommodate themselves to other Churches, to which the gospel had flowed out from them. Would to God that there were no Corinth in our times, in respect of this fault, as well as of others! But we see how savage men, who have <hi type="italic">never tasted </hi>the gospel, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.6.5">Hebrews 6:5</reference>,) trouble the Churches of the saints by a tyrannical enforcement of their own laws. <note n="887"> <div sID="gen119888" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En voulant d’vne faqon tyrannique contraindre tout le monde a receuoir leurs loix</foreign>;” — “By endeavoring, in a tyrannical way, to constrain every one to receive their laws.”<div eID="gen119888" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119886" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.14.36" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119880" osisID="1Cor.14.36" type="section"/>
entries.d1797f5df2a23407e7c379bea4a0f415b2c6ef6f: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.14.37" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.14.37" sID="gen119889" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">37.</hi> <hi type="italic">If any one thinks himself.</hi> Mark here the judgment, which he had previously assigned to the Prophets — that they should receive what they recognised as being from God. He does not, however, desire them to inquire as to his doctrine, as though it were a doubtful matter, but to receive it as the sure word of God, inasmuch as they will recognize it as the word of God, if they judge rightly. Farther, it is in virtue of apostolical authority, that he takes it upon himself to prescribe to them the sentence which they ought to pronounce. <note n="888"> <div sID="gen119891" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En cest endroit</foreign>;” — “In this case.”<div eID="gen119891" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119892" type="x-p"/>There is still greater confidence in what he immediately adds — He <hi type="italic">that is ignorant, let him be ignorant.</hi> This, it is true, was allowable for Paul, who was fully assured as to the revelation that he had received from God, and he ought also to have been well known to the Corinthians, so that they should have looked upon him in no other light, than as an Apostle of the Lord. It is not, however, for every one to advance such a claim for himself, or if he does, he will, by his boasting, throw himself open to merited derision, for <hi type="italic">then </hi>only is there ground for such confidence, when what is affirmed with the mouth shows itself in reality. It was with truth that Paul affirmed, that his precepts were those of the Lord. Many will be prepared to pretend the same thing on false grounds. His great object is this — that it may be clearly perceived, that he who does not allow himself to be under control, speaks as from the Holy Spirit, not from his own brain. That man, therefore, who is no other than a pure organ of the Holy Spirit, will have the courage to declare fearlessly with Paul, that those who shall reject his doctrine, are not <hi type="italic">Prophets </hi>or <hi type="italic">spiritual </hi>persons; and this he will do in virtue of a right that belongs to him, in accordance with what we had in the beginning of the Epistle — he <hi type="italic">that is spiritual, judgeth all things. </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.15">1 Corinthians 2:15</reference>.)<div eID="gen119892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119893" type="x-p"/>But it may be asked here, how it is that Paul declares those things to be <hi type="italic">commandments of the Lord, </hi>as to which no statement is to be found in the Scriptures? Besides this, there is also another difficulty that presents itself — that if they are the <hi type="italic">commandments of the Lord, </hi>they are necessary to be observed, and they bind the conscience, and yet they are rites connected with polity, as to the observance of which no such necessity exists. Paul, however, merely says, that he enjoins nothing, but what is in accordance with the will of God. Now God endowed him with wisdom, that he might recommend this order in external things at Corinth, and in other places — not that it might be an inviolable law, like those that relate to the spiritual worship of God, but that it might be a useful directory to all the sons of God, and not by any means to be despised.<div eID="gen119893" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.14.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119889" osisID="1Cor.14.37" type="section"/>
entries.163e31accd78083702e7a1b6647afe2ec5ff6fc8: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.14.38" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.14.38" sID="gen119894" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">38.</hi> <hi type="italic">But if any man be ignorant</hi> The old translation reads thus: <hi type="italic">He that knows not this, will be unknown;</hi> <note n="889"> <div sID="gen119896" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic"> Beausobre</hi>, when adverting to this reading, says: “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La Vulgate porte, <hi type="italic">il sera ignore</hi>, Dieu k <hi type="italic">meconnoitra</hi>;<hi type="italic"> </hi>ce qui vent dire, <hi type="italic">le punira</hi> Ce sens est fort bon</foreign>;” — “The Vulgate renders it: <hi type="italic">he will be unknown</hi> — <hi type="italic">God will disown him</hi> — meaning to say: <hi type="italic">He will punish him</hi> <hi type="italic"> </hi>This is a very good meaning.” In <hi type="italic">one </hi>Greek MS. the reading is <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀγνοεῖται</foreign>, — <hi type="italic">is unknown</hi> Wiclif, (1380) renders it — <hi type="italic">And if ony man unknowith</hi>:<hi type="italic"> he schal be unknown</hi> The view taken by Calvin, however, is the more generally approved, and seems to accord better with the general strain of the passage. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen119896" type="x-p"/> </note> but this is a mistake. For Paul had it in view to cut off every handle from contentious persons, who make no end of disputing, and that, under the pretense of inquiring — as if the matter were not yet clear; or at least he intimates in general terms, that he regarded as of no account any one that would call in question what he said. “If any one is ignorant, I do not stop to take notice of his doubts, for the certainty of my doctrine is not at all impaired thereby. Let him go then, whoever he may be. As for you, do not the less on that account give credit to Christ, as speaking by me.” In fine, he intimates, that sceptics, contentious persons, and subtle disputants; <note n="890"> <div sID="gen119897" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les sophistes qui ne font iamais que disputer, sans rien resoudre ou accorder, ne les contentieux, et subtils iaseurs</foreign>;” — “Sophists who are never but disputing, without coming to any solution or agreement, nor contentious persons, and subtile prattlers.”<div eID="gen119897" type="x-p"/> </note> do not by the questions they raise diminish, in any degree, the authority of sound doctrine, and of that truth as to which believers ought to feel assured, and at the same time he admonishes us, not to allow their doubts to be any hindrance in our way. That elevation of mind, however, which despises all human judgments, ought to be founded on ascertained truth. Hence, as it would be the part of perverse rashness, either to maintain pertinaciously, in opposition to the views of all others, an opinion that has once been taken up, or audaciously to cling to it, while others are in doubt, so, on the other hand, when we have felt assured that it is God that speaks, let us fearlessly break through all human impediments and all difficulties. <note n="891"> <div sID="gen119898" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sans nous en soucier aucunement</foreign>;” — “Without giving ourselves any concern as to them.”<div eID="gen119898" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119895" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.14.38" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119894" osisID="1Cor.14.38" type="section"/>
entries.6363e5f5b98a46ec2dc4829cd18fc4c79ee8bb67: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.14.39" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.14.39" sID="gen119899" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">39.</hi> <hi type="italic">Wherefore, brethren</hi> This is the conclusion in connection with the principal question — that <hi type="italic">prophecy </hi>is to be preferred to other gifts, because it is the most useful gift of all, while at the same time other gifts ought not to be despised. We must observe, however, his manner of speaking. For he intimates, that <hi type="italic">prophecy </hi>is worthy of being eagerly and ardently aspired at by all. In the meantime, he exhorts them not to envy others the rarer gift, <note n="892"> <div sID="gen119901" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Autres, qui ont le don des langues, qui est vn don plus rare</foreign>;” — “Others, who have the gift of tongues, which is a rarer gift.”<div eID="gen119901" type="x-p"/> </note> which is not so much to be desired; nay more, to allow them the praise that is due to them, divesting themselves of all envy.<div eID="gen119900" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.14.39" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119899" osisID="1Cor.14.39" type="section"/>
entries.ddaaae876ad1dffcf951693c6905c1dba37be7ba:
40. All things decently and in order Here we have a more general conclusion, which does not merely include, in short compass, the entire case, but also the different parts. Nay farther, it is a rule by which we must regulate
“This precept is sometimes applied to support the use of rites and ceremonies in the worship of God, not commanded in Scripture. But any one who considers the place which it holds in this discourse, will be sensible that it hath no relation to rites and ceremonies, but to the decent and orderly exercise of the spiritual gifts. Yet by parity of reasoning, it may be extended even to the rites of worship, provided they are left free to be used by every one as he sees them expedient.” — McKnight. “To adduce this text, as a direct argument about any particular external ceremonies used in divine worship, (which always appear decent and orderly to those who invent, impose, or are attached to them, and the contrary to those who dissent from them,) is doubtless wresting it from its proper meaning.” Scott. — Ed.
everything, that has to do with external polity. As he had discoursed, in various instances, as to rites, he wished to sum up everything here in a brief summary — that decorum should be observed — that confusion should be avoided. This statement shows, that he did not wish to bind consciences by the foregoing precepts, as if they were in themselves necessary, but only in so far as they were subservient to propriety and peace. Hence we gather (as I have said) a doctrine that is always in force, as to the purpose to which the polity of the Church ought to be directed. The Lord has left external rites in our choice with this view — that we may not think that his worship consists wholly in these things.
In the meantime, he has not allowed us a rambling and unbridled liberty, but has inclosed it (so to speak) with railings,
Cancellos (ut ita loquar) circumdedit. Calvin has here very probably in his eye an expression made use of by Cicero, “Si extra hos cancellos egredi conabor, quos mihi circumdedi;” — “If I shall attempt to go beyond those limits, which I have marked out for myself.” — (Cic. Quint. 10.) — Ed.
 
or at least has laid a restriction upon the liberty granted by him in such a manner, that it is after all only from his word that we can judge as to what is right. This passage, therefore, when duly considered, will show the difference between the tyrannical edicts of the Pope, which oppress men’s consciences with a dreadful bondage, and the godly regulations of the Church, by which discipline and order are maintained. Nay farther, we may readily infer from this, that the latter are not to be looked upon as human traditions, inasmuch as they are founded upon this general injunction, and have a manifest approval, as it were, from the mouth of Christ himself.

                     </ns0:gap> 29.</ns0:note> but rather that ye may prophesie <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">But rather, or principally, that you may be able to reveal the Mind and Will of God unto others. Some think by foretelling things to come; but that is not very proba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble, such an ability of prophesying being given but to few un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the New Testament: it is therefore more probable, that he speaketh of an ability to open the Scriptures, either by im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mediate Revelation (as to which they could use no means but Prayer and an holy Life) or by ordinary Meditation, and study of Scriptures. For though the former Species of Prophesying, by prediction of future things, when the truth of it was justifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by such Prophecies accomplishment, was of great use to con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firm the Doctrine of the Gospel; yet the latter was of greater and more general use for the good of others, which makes the Apostle put them upon the coveting, and earnest desire of that faculty or ability, because, of all others, it made them most eminently and generally useful to others, as well those within the Church, as those without; and thus the Apostle expound<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth himself, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:453" />2 For he that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts. 2.4. & 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.46.</ns0:note> speaketh in an <ns0:hi>unknown</ns0:hi> tongue <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">By a <ns0:hi>Tongue</ns0:hi> (for unknown is not in the <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> but necessa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rily added by our Translators, for he speaketh of such a Lan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guage) he meaneth a Language not known to all, or at least not to the most of them that hear him. It may be asked, what unknown Language the Apostle here meaneth? Shall we think that any <ns0:hi>Pastors</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Teachers</ns0:hi> in the Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> were so vain, as to preach in the <ns0:hi>Arabick, Scythian,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Part<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ian</ns0:hi> Language to a people who understood only the <ns0:hi>Greek?</ns0:hi> Our Learned <ns0:hi>Lightfoot</ns0:hi> thinks this not probable, and that if any had been so vain for ostentation, the Apostle would rather have chid them for suffering<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> such an abuse, and have forbidden such further practice, than have given direction, that if any so spake, he should interpret, as he doth <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. He rather thinks therefore, that the Apostle meaneth the <ns0:hi>Hebrew Tongue</ns0:hi>; the use of which, though it was by this time much lost through the Jews mixture with other Nations, yet was restored in a great measure to the Guides of Churches, for their better understanding the Scri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ptures of the Old Testament; and continued amongst the Jews in their reading of the Law in the Synagogues. Now there being many Jews in this Church, and the Service of God be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing ordinarily in the Jewish Synagogues performed in that Language, it is very probable, that some of these Jews that were Christianized, (to shew their skill) might, when they spake to the whole Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> use to speak in <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> though few or none understood that Language. The Apostle saith, he that did so,</ns0:note>, speaketh not unto men <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>spake not to men,</ns0:hi> that is, not to those men who did not understand that Language, not to the gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rality of his Hearers, though possibly here and there some might understand him,</ns0:note>, but unto God <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">but unto God, who being the Author of all Languages, must necessarily know the significancy of all words in them:</ns0:note>: for no man <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>areth.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> understandeth <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">For (he saith) scarce any man understood him.</ns0:note>, howbeit in the spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit he speaketh mysteries <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Howbeit he may speak mysterious things to himself, and to the understanding of his own Soul and Spirit. Others think that it was possible, that some who thus spake, being but the instruments of the holy Spirit, might not themselves understand all which they said; but that is hardly probable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 But he that prophesieth, speaketh unto men <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That is, to the understanding of men, and for the good and profit of men.</ns0:note>, to edification <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To <ns0:hi>Edification,</ns0:hi> for their increase in know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge and all habits of Grace.</ns0:note>, and exhortation <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">And <ns0:hi>Exhortation,</ns0:hi> to quicken them in the exercise and practice of such duties, as God hath, in his Word, required of them.</ns0:note>, and comfort <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">And for the relief of them under their burdens, to support and uphold their troubled or wounded Spirits. These expressions make it probable, that the Apostle, by <ns0:hi>Prophecy</ns0:hi> in this Text, understands ministerial Preaching; which more properly tends to <ns0:hi>Edification, Exhor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and <ns0:hi>Comfort,</ns0:hi> than the foretelling of things to come.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 He that speaketh in an <ns0:hi>unknown</ns0:hi> tongue, edi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fieth himself <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Knowledge or understanding of the things that any man speaketh, is necessary to the improvement of them, by their being a means to promote <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi>; for how shall what men say in the least promote, either my Faith in God or Christ, or my Love to him, if I understand not what they say? <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 10.14. <ns0:hi>How shall men believe on him of whom they have not heard?</ns0:hi> So that, though he that speaketh in an unknown Tongue, may (if he understand what he says) have his own heart affected with what he saith; yet it is not possible he should affect ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther.</ns0:note>; but he that prophesieth, edifieth the church <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">But he that preacheth in an intelligible Language and stile to all that hear him, he doth what in him lieth to edifie all those that hear him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 I would that ye all spake with tongues <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">I <ns0:hi>would</ns0:hi> in this place signifies no more than either I <ns0:hi>could wish,</ns0:hi> or I could be content that you could all speak with Tongues, if God pleased. It should seem by this speech of the Apostle's, that this speaking in unknown Tongues, was that ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />traordinary Gift, which, above all others, this Church, or the several Members of it, were proud and ambitious of. S. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> tells them, that if God pleased, he wished they could all do it.</ns0:note>, but rather that ye prophesied: for greater <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he that prophesieth, then he that speaketh with tongues, except he interpret <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">But of the two, he rather wished them all a power to open and apply the holy Scriptures to mens understandings and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />science. He addeth the reason, because it was a more honou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rable gift and work, and made men truly greater. But he adds, <ns0:hi>Except he interpret,</ns0:hi> for then he prophesied also.</ns0:note>, that the church may receive edifying <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That, saith he, the Church, that is, those that heard him prophesying, might be edified. Whence we learn, 1. That <ns0:hi>spiritual growth, and proficiency in Divine knowledge and habits of Grace,</ns0:hi> ought to be the great end of all <ns0:hi>Preachers</ns0:hi>; and whoso doth not pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pound this as his end, abuseth his Office, and trifles in a Pul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pit. 2. That whoso maketh this his end, will make it his busi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness to the best of his skill, to use such a language, stile, and method, as the generality of his Hearers may best understand; for without their understanding, there can be no edifying. And this lets us see the vanity of using much <ns0:hi>Latine,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> or a lofty stile, or a <ns0:hi>Cryptick method,</ns0:hi> not obvious to poor people in popular Sermons, where the people understand not those languages: or Philosophical ratiocinations, before a plain peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple that understand none of these thing<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. Such preaching is neither justifiable by Reason, nor by the practice either of Christ, or his Apostles.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 Now, brethren, if I come unto you speaking with tongues, what shall I profit you <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">God hath given me an ability to speak with Tongues, sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose I should come to you speaking in the <ns0:hi>Arabian, Scythian,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Parthian language,</ns0:hi> what good would it do you? How should it any way profit you?</ns0:note>, except I shall speak to you, either by <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Vers. 26.</ns0:note> revelation <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">except I should speak to you, either by <ns0:hi>Revelation,</ns0:hi> &c. Some make these four things distinct each from other: others think, that they all signifie no more, than the interpreting mentioned in the former verse. Those who distinguish them, say, By <ns0:hi>Revelation</ns0:hi> is meant the Explication of the Types and Figures of the Old Testament; or some such Revelation as <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> had in <ns0:hi>Patmos</ns0:hi>; or the expounding the Mysteries of the Gospel.</ns0:note>, or by knowledge <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Knowledge</ns0:hi> they understand the knowledge of History, or any other ordinary knowledge.</ns0:note>, or by prophecy <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Prophecy,</ns0:hi> the Explication of the difficult Texts of Scripture.</ns0:note>, or by doctrine? <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Doctrine,</ns0:hi> catechistical or practical Doctrine. But these are all but uncertain guesses; the sense is plainly no more, than if I should come speaking with unknown Tongues, and no way by interpretation make what I say intelligible unto you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 And even things without life giving sound, whether pipe, or harp, except they give a distin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction in the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Tunes.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> sounds, how shall it be known what is piped, or harped? <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">In the Sounds which are artificially made by the use of Wind-Musick, or other Musick, nothing could be understood, if Art had not also devised a distinction in the Sounds; that one Sound should signifie one thing, another Sound should signifie another thing: So unless the Voice of the Teacher be signifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cant to, and understood by the person instructed or taught, the Sound is of no use at all.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battel? <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The Trumpet is made use of in Battels, and that variously; it is used to give Souldiers notice to march on against the Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />my, and also to sound a Retreat: If there were not a distinction in the one sound, and in the other, how should the Souldier know when to go forward, and when to come back by the sound of it. To instruct them what to do, the Trumpet must not only sound, but sound intelligibly to those that hear it, which it could not, if there were no distinction in the sound.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 So likewise you, except ye utter by the tongue words easie to be <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>significant</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the air <ns0:note n="z" place="margin">By <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> is meant words which signifie well to those that hear them; for words may be significant enough in themselves, yet nothing at all significant to them that hear them, being unlearned; such sounds of words can contribute nothing to peoples knowledge, but are so much lost labour. This is a Text that deserveth the thoughts of those who affect in prea<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hing; if not the use of Languages, yet the use of a <ns0:hi>Stile,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Method,</ns0:hi> which no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> one of many of those who hear them, understand. It is all one to speak in an unknown Tongue, as in a stile, or method that people do not understand; and truly, such are the generality of Ministers Hearers, that words most significant in themselves, and to learned Ears, are least significant to them, being hardest to be understood; so as they know nothing of what they say, and the Minister doth but, as to the far greater number of people, beat the air (which is a dreadful meditation.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:454" />10 There are, it may be, so many kinds of voi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces in the world, and none of them <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> without signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fication <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The whole Earth was originally of one Language and of one Speech, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 11.1. But upon the building of <ns0:hi>Babel, v.</ns0:hi> 7. God confounded their Languages, so as they did not understand one another. They being scattered abroad, had different Lan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guages; so as now there are in the World many Languages, and the words in every Language are significant to those that under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand that Language.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be to him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> a barbarian unto me <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">But if a man doth not understand the Language, the words are not significant unto him, I shall neither understand him, nor will he understand me; for a <ns0:hi>Barbarian</ns0:hi> cannot understand one of another Nation, till he hath learned the Language of that Nation<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> nor can a man of another Nation understand a <ns0:hi>Barba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rian,</ns0:hi> till he hath learned his Language.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Even so ye, forasmuch as ye are zealous of <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>Spirits.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> spiritual <ns0:hi>gifts</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This proves that the Members of the Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> were very ambitious of spiritual gifts. The Particle <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which our Translation here renders <ns0:hi>so,</ns0:hi> plainly signifies <ns0:hi>therefore</ns0:hi> in this place. In the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> it is <ns0:hi>because,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>forasmuch as ye are zealous of Spirits,</ns0:hi> the Efficient is put for the Effect, the Spirit which is the Author of those gifts for the gifts themselves.</ns0:note>, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Seek that ye may excel in them, and that will be, if you most desire those which tend to the edifying the Church, and use those with which God hath blessed you in the best order and manner for that end. From whence it is observable, That the im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />provement of the people, to whom we preach in the know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge of God, and in Faith and Obedience, is the great end which we ought to propose to our selves in the discharge of our Office, and in the use of our Gifts.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Wherefore let him that speaketh in an <ns0:hi>un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />known</ns0:hi> tongue, pray that he may interpret <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To <ns0:hi>interpret</ns0:hi> here signifieth no more<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> than to render that intelligible to people, which he first uttereth in an unknown Tongue. But what need he pray for that? Hath not every man, that can speak, a power to speak his native Language, as well as a foreign Language? Some say therefore, that <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> in this place signifies <ns0:hi>also.</ns0:hi> Let him pray, and also interpret; but this seemeth hard: nor can I think those that had a faculty to speak in an unknown Tongue, might some of them not themselves understand what they said, and so had need to pray that they might interpret: But they might be pufft up with their gift, and think it beneath them to interpret, and then they had need to pray, that they might have humility enough to inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pret. Others think, that by <ns0:hi>interpreting</ns0:hi> in this place, is meant something more than bare translating, or turning the words into the common Language of the place, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the opening and ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plying of the Scriptures, an ability to which was a distinct gift; which they who would have, had need pray, that God would open their eyes to understand the Mysteries of his Law.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 For if I pray in an <ns0:hi>unknown</ns0:hi> tongue, my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">From this and the former verse, the Papists would justifie the lawfulness of their Latine Service, which none or few of the common people understand; and they seem to have a little advantage from the Opinion of some of the Ancients, That some of those who spake with Tongues, did not themselves un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand what they uttered, but the Spirit of God only made use of their Tongues as <ns0:hi>Machins.</ns0:hi> But these are apprehensi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons much beneath the Spirit of Light and Truth, that it should make use of the tongue of a man for an end neither profitable to the man himself, nor others. Besides, how is it then true which we had, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4. That <ns0:hi>he who spake in an unknown tongue, edifieth himself?</ns0:hi> Nay, how can it be true, which is here said, That such a mans <ns0:hi>Spirit</ns0:hi> prayeth? Nor is it here said, <ns0:hi>My Vn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstanding</ns0:hi> is <ns0:hi>dark</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>blind,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>unfruitful</ns0:hi>; that is, though my self understand, yet my knowledge bringeth forth no fruit to the advantage or good of others. <ns0:hi>My Spirit prayeth,</ns0:hi> but others cannot pray with me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 What is it then? I will pray with the spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">What is to be done then? <ns0:hi>I will</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle) <ns0:hi>pray with the Spirit,</ns0:hi> that is, either use the extraordinary influences of the Spirit of God upon me: or with my own Spirit, with the inward attention of my thoughts, and the utmost intension of my mind, and the greatest devotion and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ervour of affecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons.</ns0:note>, and I will pray with the understanding al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">But I will so pray, that my self and others may under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand what I say, I will neither so pray, that my self shall not understand what I say, nor yet so, that others shall not under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand me. <ns0:hi>Vnderstanding</ns0:hi> is here taken in a Passive sense, though the Active sense of the term be not to be excluded.</ns0:note>: also <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 47.7. Eph. 5.19. Col. 3. 16.</ns0:note> I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The same thing he also saith of Singing, to let us know, That all our religious Acts in publick Assemblies, ought to be so performed, that others may be benefited by them, which they cannot be, if they do not understand what we say, whether it be in <ns0:hi>preach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, praying,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>singing.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Else, when thou shalt bless with the spirit <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Blessing is expounded in the latter part of the verse, <ns0:hi>gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving of thanks</ns0:hi> to God, which is either <ns0:hi>in Prayer,</ns0:hi> (for Thanks<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />giving is a part of Prayer) or <ns0:hi>in singing of Psalms.</ns0:hi> Blessing with the Spirit either signifieth giving of thanks with the inward man, or <ns0:hi>giving of thanks</ns0:hi> in an unknown Tongue, by the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />traordinary influence of the Spirit of God.</ns0:note>, how shall he that occupieth the room of the un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />learned, say Amen at thy giving of thanks <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">It is plain from hence, 1. That the Teachers had in the Apostolical Churches distinct places and seats from the common Hearers, for their better conveniency in speaking, that they might so speak, as all might hear, understand, and be profited. 2. That in those Churches there was one only who used to speak audibly, and the work of the others was only from a devout heart to say <ns0:hi>Amen,</ns0:hi> wishing or praying, that God would do what in the name of all, he that ministred, had asked of God for them. So 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 16.36. <ns0:hi>Nehem.</ns0:hi> 5.13. & 8.6. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 106.48.</ns0:note>, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest? <ns0:note n="⸫" place="bottom">Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple ought not to say <ns0:hi>Amen</ns0:hi> to any thing, but to understand that Petition, or those Petitions to which, in the Worship of God, they added their <ns0:hi>Amen,</ns0:hi> which word made the Petitions theirs, being a Particle of <ns0:hi>wishing,</ns0:hi> as well as <ns0:hi>affirming.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 For thou verily givest thanks well: but the other is not edified <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Otherwise, saith the Apostle, it is possible, <ns0:hi>that thou mayest give thanks well</ns0:hi>; but others get no good by it, nor can make any good and spiritual improvement of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 I thank my God, I speak with tongues more then you all <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Our Saviour, in the Parable of the good Shepherd, gives us this as his Character, That <ns0:hi>the sheep hear his voice, and follow him</ns0:hi>; and we shall observe this great Apostle every where pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pounding himself for imitation to them. They are bad Shep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />herds over Gods Flock, that must only be heard, but not fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowed. The Apostle lets them know, That God had not left him without the gift of speaking with divers Tongues, nay, he had it in a more eminent manner than they all, put them all together, they could not speak with so many Tongues as he did.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that <ns0:hi>by my voice</ns0:hi> I might teach others also, then ten thousand words in an <ns0:hi>unknown</ns0:hi> tongue <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Yet he had so great a regard to the end of his Ministry, teaching others, and communicating Divine knowledge to them, that he had rather speak a little tending to that end, than never so much in a Language, which those to whom he spake, did not understand.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 Brethren, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 131.2. Matt. 11.25. & 18.3. Rom. 16.19.</ns0:note> be not children in understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">In Understanding the differences of gifts, and which are more excellent, or of the right use of gifts.</ns0:note> howbeit in malice <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 2.6.</ns0:note> be ye children: but in understanding be <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>perfect, or of ripe age.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> men <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">You are com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded indeed in something to be like little children, <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 18.3. but it is not to be understood with relation to knowledge and understanding, but with reference to innocence and malice, which is opposite to it; ye ought to study to be men in un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstanding, though with respect to innocence, ye ought to be as little children.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 In the Law it is written <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">By the Law here is meant the Old Testament, (as in many other Texts, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 10.34. and 15.25.) so called (as some think) in opposition to the words of the Scribes. The words following are quoted out of <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 28.11, 12. <ns0:hi>For with stammer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing lips and another tongue will he speak to this people. To whom he said, This is the rest wherewith ye may cause the weary to rest, and this is the refreshing, yet they would not hear.</ns0:hi> But there is nothing more ordinary, than for the Penmen of the Scriptures of the New Testament to quote passages out of the Old, keep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing not so much to the words, as to the sense; nor quoting them all, but so many of them as serve for their purposes. The words in the Prophet are a threatning, that because God had brought the Jews into <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> and promised them rest there, upon their obedience to his Commandments, and they would not hear, he would now take another course with them, speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to them with men of stammering lips, and of another Lan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guage; meaning the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Babylonians,</ns0:hi> with whom in Captivity they conversed afterwards for seventy years. The sense is much the same (as some think.) For they that speak to others in and with strange Tongues, are like those that stam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer at others, which looks more like a mocking them, than an instructing them. Others make the <ns0:hi>gift of Tongues,</ns0:hi> under the <ns0:hi>New Testament,</ns0:hi> to be within the Prophecy of <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi>; as if the Prophets words contained both a threatning, to speak to the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> with the strange Tongues of the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi>; and a promise under the Gospel; to speak to them with the Tongues of the Apostles and others, tuned to various Tunes, as men of several Nations could understand. Others make this the sense, as if the Prophet complained, That the people were so mad, that they regarded no more God speaking to them, than they would have regarded one chattering with a strange Tongue. And they think, the Apostle checks them for being so ambi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tious of speaking with <ns0:hi>strange Tongues,</ns0:hi> whenas their being so spoken to, was by the Prophet threatned as a judgment upon them.</ns0:note> With <ns0:hi>men of</ns0:hi> o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther tongues and other lips, will I speak to this people <ns0:hi>s</ns0:hi>: and yet for all that they will not hear me, saith the Lord <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And yet they will not <ns0:hi>hear me,</ns0:hi> nor hearken to, and obey me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:454" />22 Wherefore tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Wherefore tongues are for a sign,</ns0:hi> &c. that is, an eminent pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duct of Divine Providence for the confirmation of the Truth of the Doctrine of the Gospel; signifying, that the Doctrine which was so delivered in every Nations language, must be from Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven, from whence the first Ministers must have their power so to speak; yet doubtless, they were not only for a sign, being also a means, by which the knowledge of the Gospel was con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veyed unto those who could not have understood what the Apostles and first Ministers of the Gospel said, had they not spoken to them in the Language of the Hearers.</ns0:note>: but prophecy <ns0:hi>serveth</ns0:hi> not for them that believe not, but for them that believe <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">When he saith, <ns0:hi>Prophesying</ns0:hi> serveth <ns0:hi>not for them that believe not:</ns0:hi> the mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing is, not <ns0:hi>only</ns0:hi> for them that believe not; for prophesying is certainly of use for them that believe not, for their conversion, as well as for them that believe for their edification.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 If therefore the whole church be come toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther into one place <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Phrase signifieth to <ns0:hi>one place,</ns0:hi> or for <ns0:hi>one and the same work</ns0:hi>; the first seemeth to be meant here by what followeth.</ns0:note>, and all speak with tongues <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Some think that the Apostle here, by <ns0:hi>all speaking with Tongues,</ns0:hi> understands all, or many of them, confusedly talking together; and indeed that is an errour: we shall find the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle afterward reflecting upon them for; but here I do not think it is intended, but only many of you, one after another, because of what the Apostle speaketh of <ns0:hi>Prophesying, v.</ns0:hi> 24. For if <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> prophesied in that sense, talking at the same time toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther confusedly, and an Unbeliever came in and heard, they would also, instead of being convinced, say they were mad.</ns0:note>, and there come in those that are unlearned, or un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />believers <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">One that is an Heathen, or that did not understand the Lan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guage you discoursed in,</ns0:note>, will they not say ye are mad? <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">would he not say you were men that had lost the use of your Reason, to talk to men in a Lan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guage you your selves knew they understood nothing of?</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 But if all prophesie <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>All</ns0:hi> here certainly is not to be understood of every one in the Assembly, for all were not Prophets, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.29. nor could the speaking of a great number be judged orderly by the Light of Nature: it here must signifie <ns0:hi>any,</ns0:hi> one, or more, suc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessively, interpret or apply the holy Scriptures.</ns0:note>, and there come in one that believeth not, or <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> unlearned, he is convin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ced of all <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thens will see an order in this, and will stand still to hear and be convinced.</ns0:note>, he is judged of all <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Seeing their wicked life, and false Religion judged, and condemned by all those that so prophesie.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 And thus are the secrets of his heart made manifest <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">God either, by an extraordinary Providence discovering to him that prophesieth, the secrets of such a sinners heart, and causing him that prophesieth to make them manifest; or by a more ordinary Providence (often experienced at this day) directing the Preacher to such Subjects and Discourses, as he that cometh to hear shall think directed to himself, and confess that he is the man.</ns0:note>, and so falling down on <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> face, he will worship God <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">and be convinced of his errours, and converted, and turn to the Christian Religion, and report that God indeed is amongst you. S<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>as Prophesying will have these two great advantages of speaking with Tongues, God will be more glorified, and the Souls of others will be more profited, (which makes the gift of Prophesying much preferable to the gift of Tongues.)</ns0:note>, and report <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 45.14. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.23.</ns0:note> that God is in you of a truth <ns0:hi>g.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 How is it then, brethren? When ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 12. 8, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">By what followeth in the two next verses, one would think that some of them, in their Church-meetings, were so ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />surd, as being endued with several gifts, they would be using them all together; one singing, another preaching, a third speaking with Tongues, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> But this is so apparent a confusi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, that one must be very uncharitable to this famous Church, to presume that they should be so absurd. Others therefore rather think, that those endued with several gifts, (of which he reckoneth five) under which he comprehendeth all others) were every one contending for his course to exercise his gift; one for spending the time in singing the Psalm he had made; another for spending the time in hearing his doctrinal discourse; a third for the spending it in hearing him discourse in an un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />known Tongue; a fourth for the spending it in hearing his Revelation; a fifth for the spending it in hearing his Interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation, or at least desiring the time might be protracted, until they had been all successively heard.</ns0:note>: Let all things be done to edifying <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To prevent this and other disorders, the Apostle giveth several Rules. The first is, That all things should be so done, as might tend best to promote in men Faith and Holiness; that is, and ought to be the main and chief end of those who any way minister in Sacred things.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 If any man speak in <ns0:hi>an unknown</ns0:hi> tongue, <ns0:hi>let it be</ns0:hi> by two, or at the most <ns0:hi>by</ns0:hi> three, and that <ns0:hi>by</ns0:hi> course, and let one interpret <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Concerning the use of their gift of Tongues, he directeth three things: 1. That every one that had it, should not be am<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bitious to shew it at all times, but two or three at most at a time. 2. That they should do it by course, not together, con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fusedly. 3. Not without one to interpret, that people might un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand. For though these were extraordinary gifts, flowing from a more than ordinary influence of the Spirit of God; yet they were abiding habits, not coming upon them at some cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain times, by an impulse; for then they would not have been under humane Government, as it is apparent this gift of tongues was, else <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> could not have so governed himself in the use of it, as he lets us know he did, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 But if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">If he hath a mind to use this gift, he may use it to God, who understands all Languages by himself;</ns0:note>, and let him speak to him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, and to God <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">but let him keep silence, in the Assembly of Christians, where he is not under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the others judge <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">That is, two or three successively, the one beginning to speak when the others have done, and two or three at the same Church-Assembly; and if there be more present, let them sit still and judge of the truth of what he saith.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 If <ns0:hi>any thing</ns0:hi> be revealed to another that sit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teth by, let the first hold his peace <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">There were two modes or sorts of Prophecies; the one or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinary, when the Teachers came to those Assemblies furnished with a <ns0:hi>Revelation</ns0:hi> from some previous impression of God upon him, inabling him to give the sense of some Scripture, or to open some Divine Truth; not as we are, but by some influence of the holy Spirit upon him, without the use of such means as we use. The other was, by some present <ns0:hi>afflatus</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>impression:</ns0:hi> the Apostle seems not to speak of the latter, or if of both, he plainly lets them know, that even such a one was under the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vernment of natural Order, and obliged to do nothing confu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sedly and tumultuously, but might, without any offence to God, stay until the other had finished his Discourse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 For ye may all prophesie one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Ye may not all prophesie in the same day, or hour, or mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of time, but orderly and successively, ye may all prophe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sie, the end of it being for the instruction and consolation of all, which may mind you so to govern your selves in the exercise of that gift, as not to lose your end, but all may learn, and may be comforted. Which lets us know, that though their recei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving the gift of Prophecy obliged them to an exercise of it, yet it did not oblige them to an exercise of it, in or at this or that particular time.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">By the <ns0:hi>Spirits of the Prophets</ns0:hi> the Apostle either meaneth their <ns0:hi>spiritual Gifts,</ns0:hi> as to the use and exercise of them, and the actions to be done by them; or the actions themselves, or in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpretations pretendedly done and given, by the exercise of those Gifts, their Doctrines: Or thirdly, That Instinct, or <ns0:hi>Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />petus,</ns0:hi> by which they pretend themselves to be moved to pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phesie, these (he saith) are subject to the Prophets themselves, so as they may themselves govern their Gifts, or (which most think is the rather here intended) they are subject to the judgment and censure of others that are endued with the same Gift. But here ariseth a difficulty, how the Gifts of the holy Spirit, flowing immediately from the Spirit, should be subject to any humane judgment or censure? This indeed they could not, if the Divine Revelation to this or that man were full and perfect, and ran as clearly in the stream always, as it was in the fountain. But God giveth his Spirit to us but by measure, and in the exercise of our gifts there is always <ns0:hi>aliquid hawani,</ns0:hi> some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing of our own, and this maketh them <ns0:hi>subject to the Prophets: viz.</ns0:hi> whether what they pretended to have from the Spirit of God, were indeed from it yea or no? Prophets were obliged to prohesie, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.6. but <ns0:hi>according to the Analogy of saith.</ns0:hi> Now whether they did so or no, might be judged by other Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phets, according to that Rule. Others think this Text is to be interpreted restrainedly, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> As to this thing in this matter of plain, natural order, commanding, whiles one speaks, all the rest to hold their peace.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:455" />33 For God is not <ns0:hi>the author</ns0:hi> of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, '<ns0:hi>tumult,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>unquietness.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> confusion, but of peace, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 11.16.</ns0:note> as in all churches of the Saints <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Here he sheweth the Principle upon which he said, That the Spirits of the Prophets are subject to the Prophets: what any Prophets speak is not so certain, or at least not more cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain, than this, That nothing, which is confusion, can be from God. Now for two or three to speak together in a publick Assembly, is a confusion, and a breach of order, of which God cannot be the Author: therefore in such a thing as that, the Spirits of the Prophets must be subject to other Prophets; and there is a general Rule which concerneth not only the Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> but all Churches.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 Let your women keep silence in the chur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ches for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 11.3. Eph. 5.23. Col. 3.18. 1 Pet. 3.1.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>they are commanded</ns0:hi> to be under obedience: as also saith the Law <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This Rule must be restrained to <ns0:hi>ordinary Prophesyings:</ns0:hi> For certainly, if the Spirit of Prophecy came upon a Woman in the Church, she might speak. <ns0:hi>Anna,</ns0:hi> who was a Prophetess, in the Temple, <ns0:hi>gave thanks to the Lord, and spake of him to all them that looked for Redemption in Israel:</ns0:hi> and I cannot tell how <ns0:hi>Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lips</ns0:hi> Daughters <ns0:hi>prophesied,</ns0:hi> if they did not speak in the presence of many, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 21.9. The reason that is given, why women should keep silence, is, because they are commanded to be in obedience. This Apostle speaketh much the same thing, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.11, 12. because it looked like an usurping authority over the man; which indeed is true, if it had been the ordina<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry practice of women to speak in the Assemblies of the Church; but not so, if some particular women sometimes spake upon an extraordinary impulse or impression. The Law to which the Apostle here refers, is thought to be that, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 3.16. where the woman is commanded to be subject to her husband, and it is said, that <ns0:hi>he should rule over her:</ns0:hi> yet that Law did neither restrain <ns0:hi>Miriam</ns0:hi> from prophesying, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 15.20. nor yet <ns0:hi>Hul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dah,</ns0:hi> to whom <ns0:hi>Iosiah</ns0:hi> himself sent, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 34.22. of whom it is also said, <ns0:hi>That she dwelt in the Colledge</ns0:hi>; but setting aside that extraordinary case of a special <ns0:hi>Afflatus,</ns0:hi> it was doubtless unlawful for a woman to speak in the Church.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home: for it is a shame for women to speak in the church <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">This must be understood of speaking to the Congregation, for the Instructing them, or speaking in the Congregation to the Minister, or any of the people, for her own instruction. For the woman might doubtless say <ns0:hi>Amen</ns0:hi> to the publick Pray<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers, and also sing with the Congregation to the honour and glory of God. But for her to speak in an ordinary course of Prophecy to instruct people, or to call aloud to the Minister, or any Members in the Assembly of the Church, to be satisfied in any thing wherein she was in doubt, this she is forbidden.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 What? came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only? <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">These words look like a smart reflection upon divers Mem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bers of this <ns0:hi>Church</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> who thought themselves wiser than all the World besides; and the Apostle might foresee, that out of the high opinion they had of themselves, they would much contemn and slight his directions. He therefore asks them, what they thought of themselves? Whether they thought themselves the only Churches in the World, or were the first that believed in Christ? so that the Gospel went out from them, and they might give Law to all Churches? There were Chur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ches at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and in several other places, before there was any Church at <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> so as the Gospel came unto them from other Churches, and did not go out from them to other Churches.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 10.7. 1 Joh. 4.6.</ns0:note> If any man think himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things that I write unto you, are the commandments of the Lord <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">If there be any amongst you who hath a conceit, that he is inspired by God, and from that inspiration understandeth the Mind and Will of God, he must acknowledge, that I also am an Apostle, and know the Mind and Will of God as well as he; and being so, that what I tell you, is the Commandment of the Lord.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 But if any man be ignorant, let him be igno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rant <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">If any one will pretend ignorance in this, he is wilfully ignorant; for my own part I will concern my self no further about him, but leave my self and him also to the Judgment of God, <ns0:hi>Let him be ignorant.</ns0:hi> In some Copies it is, <ns0:hi>He shall not be known.</ns0:hi> In the Day of Judgment Christ shall say unto him, <ns0:hi>De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />part from me, I know you not.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesie, and forbid not to speak with tongues <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The Apostle concludeth his Discourse, summarily repeat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing all that he before had said. He had, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2. incouraged their <ns0:hi>desire</ns0:hi> of spiritual gifts; all along the Chapter he hath been mag<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifying the gift of <ns0:hi>Prophecy</ns0:hi> above the gift of Tongues, as being of much more general use, and more for the profit of others; but he minds them here, that he did not forbid those for whom God had given the gift of Tongues, to make use of it at due times, and in a due manner and order.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 Let all things be done decently, and in or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He forbad them not to speak with Tongues, provided they did it decently and orderly, as all other things ought to be done in so grave an Assembly, as that of the Church, and in so grave an Action, as the Worship of God. For <ns0:hi>Women to pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phesie</ns0:hi> in the publick Assemblies, was an undecent thing, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 35. he had said, that <ns0:hi>it was a shame.</ns0:hi> For many of them to speak together, confusedly, making a noise, that was <ns0:hi>disorderly</ns0:hi>; nor did this decency or indecency, order or disorder, arise from obeying or disobeying the Apostolical Constitution, but from the Law of God, the Light of Nature, the common usage of all the Churches of Christians, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 33. All things ought so be done, (especially in Religious Assemblies and Actions) as they may not be judged by the Law of God, or the Light of Nature, or the common custom of other Churches, to be done inde<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cently or confusedly, without order. It is very observable, That though the Apostle, in these things, hath given Rules, yet he hath determined nothing shameful or uncomely, but what he hath made to appear so, either from the Divine Law, (as in the case of the womens prophesying, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 34.) or from Nature and Reason, (as in the case of many speaking at the same time) it being useless to the end, which was teaching and instructing those to whom they spake, and what Unbelievers would count the effect of madness, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 23.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
